Die Res flexionsbestimmung von Kraft ist es hier, was ein- 1 mal für den Verstand fixirt und als ein Lektes dasteht, ihn daher hindert und es fur überſluſſig halten läßt, weiter nach dem Begriffe zu fragen. Aber dieß wenigstens schwebt ihm gedankenlos, vor, daß die Wirkung der Kraft etwas reelles, sinnfäl liges ist, und daß in der Kraft das ist, was in ihrer Aeusserung, auch daß die Kraft eben diese Kraft ihrer Aeusserung durch das Verhältniß der ideellen - Momente, des Raums und der Zeit, erlangt. Es gehört ferner auch zu dies ser begrifflosen Reflexion, die sogenannten Kräfte der Materie als eingepflanzt, und als ihr ur sprunglich äusserlich anzusehen, so daß eben diese Identität der Zeit und des Raums, welche bey der Reflexionsbestimmung von Krast vorschwebt und welche in Wahrheit das Wesen der Materie ausmacht, als etwas ihr Fremdes und Zufa liges gesekt ist.
e: The transition from ideality to reality, from abstraction to concrete determinate being, here from space and time to the reality that appears as matter, is incomprehensible for the understanding, and therefore always makes itself external for it, and as something given. The familiar representation is to let space and time, as empty, be filled from outside with matter, and, on the one hand, in this way to assume material things as indifferent to space and time, and on the other hand at the same time as essentially spatial and temporal. — What is usually said of matter is, α) that it is composite; — this refers to its identity with space. Insofar as abstraction is made in it from time and in general from all form, it has been asserted of it that it is eternal and unalterable. This follows in fact immediately; but such a matter is also only an untrue abstraction. β) Matter is impenetrable and offers resistance, is something tangible, visible, etc. These predicates are nothing other than that matter is, on the one hand, for determinate perception, in general for an other, but on the other hand just as much for itself. Both are determinations which it has precisely as the identity of space and time, of the immediate outside-one-another and of negativity or of becoming. — The transition of ideality into reality occurs, however, also in a more formal manner in the best-known mechanical phenomena, namely that the [p. 141] ideality can take the place of reality and conversely; and it is only the usual thoughtlessness of representation and of the understanding that is to blame for the fact that for them their identity does not emerge from this interchangeability of the two. In the lever, e.g., mass can be put in the place of distance and conversely, and a quantum of the ideal moment produces the same effect as the corresponding real. — In the magnitude of motion, likewise, velocity, the quantitative relationship of space and time, takes the place of the mass, and conversely the same real effect comes forth when the latter is increased and the former proportionally diminished. — A brick by itself does not strike a man dead, but produces this effect only through the velocity attained, i.e., the man is struck dead by space and time. — It is the determination of reflection of force that here, once it is fixed for the understanding and stands there as an ultimate, therefore hinders it and lets it hold it superfluous to inquire further after the Concept. But at least this hovers before it thoughtlessly: that the effect of the force is something real, evident to the senses, and that in the force there is what is in its expression, also that the force attains precisely this force of its expression through the relationship of the ideal moments, of space and time. — It belongs, further, also to this conceptless reflection to regard the so-called forces of matter as implanted, and as originally external to it, so that precisely this identity of time and space, which hovers before one in the determination of reflection of force and which in truth constitutes the essence of matter, is posited as something alien to it and contingent.

o: 3 weyter Theil. Die Physik. S. 204. Die Materie hält sich in ihr selbst durch das Mo. ment ihrer Negativität, Verschiedenheit oder abstrakter Vereinzelung auseinander; sie hat Repulsion. Ihre Aussereinander ist aber eben so wesentlich, weil diese Verschiedenen ein und dasselbe sind, die negative - Einheit dieses aussereinandersenen den Fürsichseyns, somit continuirlich. Die Materie hat daher Attraction. Die Einheit dieser Momente ist die Schwere.
e: §. 204. Matter holds itself asunder in itself through the moment of its negativity, diversity or abstract individuation; it has repulsion. Its outside-one-another, however, is just as essential, because these diverse ones are one and the same, the negative unity of this being-for-itself that is outside-one-another, — hence continuous. Matter therefore has attraction. The unity of these moments is gravity.

o: Kant hat unter andern auch das Verdienst, durch seinen Versuch einer sogenannten Construction der Materie, in seinen metaphysischen Anfangsgründen der Naturwissenschaft, den Anfang zu einem Begriff der Materie gemacht zu haben, nachdem sie vorher nur als ein Todtes des Verstandes zu Grunde gelegen hatte, und ihre Bestimmungen, in dem Verhältnissevon Eigensch a ften aufgefaßt worden waren. Mit diesem Versuche hat Kant den Begriff der Naturphilosophie erweckt, welche nichts anders ist, als das Begreifen der Natur, oder was dasselbe ist, die Erkenntniß des Begriffes in der Natur. Er hat aber dabey die Reflexionsbestimmungen von Attractivkraft und Repulsivkraft als fertige angenommen, und wies der bey Bestimmung derselben, aus welchen die Mas terie hervorgehensoute, diese als ein fertiges voraussekt, eine Verwirrung, die eine nothwendige Folge ist, weil jene abstracten Momente ohne ihre Identität nicht begriffen werden können, oder viele mehr weil die Betrachtung dieser entgegengesekten Bestimmungen sich unmittelbar in ihre Identitat auf. löst. Ausführlicher habe ich die in dieser Kantischen [p. 143] Exposition herrschende Verwirrung, in meinem Sy stem der Logik, ir. Band ir. Th. S. 119 ff. darge. fte ut. 4.§. 205. Die Materie ist als schwer nur erst) 1 die in sich seyende, oder allgemeine Materie; sie ist 1 der Gegenstand der Mechanik. Aber dieser Begriff muß sich 2) specificiren; so ist sie die elementa. rische Materie, und Gegenstand der elementari schen Physik. 3) Die besondere Materie sich in die Einzelnheit zusammennehmend ist die individua lisierte Materie, und Gegenstand der Physik der ei gentlichen Körperwelt. Die Mechanik, §. 206. Die Materie hat zunächst als bloß allgemeine, nur einen quantitativen Unterschied -, und besondert sich in verschiedene Quanta, Massen, welche in der oberflächlichen Bestimmung eines Ganzen oder Eins, Köre per sind. §. 207. Der Körper ist) 1 als schwere Materie die ges diegene Identität des Raums und der Zeit, aber 2) als die erste Negation hat er ihre von einander und von ihm unterschiedene Idealität an ihm und ist wesent lich im Raume und in der Zeit, deren gegen diese Form gleichgültigen Inhalt er ausmacht.
e: Kant has, among other things, also the merit of having made, by his attempt at a so-called construction of matter, in his Metaphysical Foundations of Natural Science, the beginning of a Concept of matter, after it had previously lain at the basis only as a dead thing of the understanding, and its determinations had been grasped in the relationship of properties. — With this attempt Kant awakened the Concept of philosophy of nature, which is nothing other than the comprehending of nature, or, what is the same, the cognition of the Concept in nature. In this, however, he accepted the determinations of reflection of attractive force and repulsive force as ready-made, and again, in determining these, out of which matter was to proceed, presupposed it as something ready-made, — a confusion that is a necessary consequence, because those abstract moments cannot be comprehended without their identity, or rather because the consideration of these opposed determinations dissolves immediately into their identity. I have presented more fully the confusion prevailing in this Kantian [p. 143] exposition, in my System of Logic, vol. 1, part 1, p. 119 ff. §. 205. Matter, as heavy, is at first only 1) the matter that is within itself, or universal matter; it is the object of mechanics. But this Concept must 2) specify itself; thus it is elemental matter, and object of elemental physics. 3) Particular matter, gathering itself together into singularity, is individualized matter, and object of the physics of the proper world of bodies. A. §. 206. Matter has at first, as merely universal, only a quantitative difference, and particularizes itself into different quanta, — masses, which in the superficial determination of a whole or one are bodies. §. 207. The body is 1) as heavy matter the solid identity of space and time, but 2) as the first negation it has in it their ideality, distinguished from one another and from it, and is essentially in space and in time, whose content, indifferent to this form, it constitutes.

o: §. 208. [p. 144] fälliges Eins, 5) aber ist er die beyde in ihrer Entgegenseßung bindende Einheit; so hat er wesentlich Bez wegung, die Erscheinung der Schwere. Wie die Kräfte als der Materie nur einge pflanzt angesehen worden, so ist es insbesondere auch die Bewegung, welche selbst in der wissenschaftlich seyn sollenden Physik, als eine dem Körper äusserliche Bestimmung betrachtet wird;, so daß es ein Haupt Axiom der Mechanik ist, daß der Körper schlechthin nur durch eine äusserliche Ur sache in Bewegung als in einen Zustand versekt werden soll. Einerseits ist es der Verstand, welcher Bewegung und Ruhe als begrifflose Bestimmungen auseinander hält, und deswegen ihr Uebergehen in einander nicht erfaßt, andererseits schweben der Vorstellung nur die selbstlosen Körper der Erde vor, die der Gegenstand der gemeinen Mechanik sind. Die Bestimmungen, welche an der Erschei nung solcher Körper vorkommen und gelten, werdenzu Grunde gelegt, und die Natur der selbstständigen Körper darunter subsumirt; wogegen in Wahrheit diese vielmehr die allgemeinen und jene die schlecht hin subsumirten sind, und in der absoluten Mechanik sich der Begriffs in seiner Wahrheit und eigens thumlich darstellt. : §. 209. In der Bewegung sekt sich die Zeit räumlich alsOrt, aber diese gleichgültige Räumlichkeit wird ebenso unmittelbar zeitlich; der Ort wird ein anderer ( §.202.) Diese Differenz der Zeit und des Raums ist als Unterschied ihrer absoluten Einheit, des gleichgültigen Inhalts, ein Unterschied von Körpern, welche sich auseinander halten, - und ebensosehr durch, ihre Schwere ihre Einheit suchen; allgemeine: Gravitation.
e: §. 208. [p. 144] one, 5) but it is the unity binding the two in their opposition; thus it essentially has motion, the appearance of gravity. Just as the forces have been regarded as merely implanted in matter, so it is in particular also motion that, even in the physics that is supposed to be scientific, is considered as a determination external to the body; so that it is a main axiom of mechanics that the body is absolutely to be put into motion, as into a state, only by an external cause. On the one hand it is the understanding that holds motion and rest apart as conceptless determinations, and therefore does not grasp their passing over into one another; on the other hand, only the selfless bodies of the earth, which are the object of ordinary mechanics, hover before representation. The determinations that occur and hold in the appearance of such bodies are taken as a basis, and the nature of the independent bodies is subsumed under them; whereas in truth the latter are rather the universal ones and the former the absolutely subsumed ones, and in absolute mechanics the Concept presents itself in its truth and in its own peculiar way. §. 209. In motion time posits itself spatially as place, but this indifferent spatiality becomes just as immediately temporal; the place becomes an other (§ 202). This difference of time and space is, as the difference of their absolute unity, of the indifferent content, a difference of bodies, which hold themselves apart from one another and just as much seek their unity through their gravity; — universal gravitation.

o: §. 210. Die Gravitation ist der wahrhafte und bestimmte Begriff der materiellen Körperlichkeit, die damit ebenso wesentlich in besondere Körper getheilt ist, und 1 ihr erscheinendes Daseyn, das Moment der äusserlichen Einzelnheit, in der Bewegung hat, welche hiedurch unmittelbar als eine Relation mehrerer Köra per bestimmt ist. 1 Die allgemeine Gravitation muß für sich als ein tiefer Gedanke anerkannt werden, der eine absolute Grundlage für die Mechanik ausmacht, wenn er schen zunächst in der Sphäre der Reflexion gefaßt, die Aufmerksamkeit und Zutrauen vornemlich durch die damit verbundene quantitative Bestimmung auf sich zog, und seine Bewährung nur in der vom Sonnensystem bis auf die Erscheinung der Haarrörchenherab verfolgten Erfahrung finden sollte. Uebrigens widerspricht die Gravitation unmittelbar dem Geseke der Trägheit, denn vermöge jener strebtdie Materie aus sich selbst zur anderen hin. Im Begriffe der Schwere sind, wie gezeigt, selbst die beyden Momente des Fürsichseyns, und der das Fürsichseyn aufhebenden Continuität enthalten. Diese Momente des Begriffs erfahren nun das Schicksal, als besondere Kräfte, entsprechend der Attractivund Repulsivkraft, in näherer Bestimmung als Centripetalund Centrifugalkraft gefaßt zu werden, die wie die Schwere auf die Körper agiren, unabhängig von einander und zufälligerweise in einem Dritten, dem Körper, zusammenstofsen sollen. Hiedurch wird, was am Gedanken der Schwere Tiefes ist, wieder zu nichte gemacht, und so lange kann Begriff und Vernunft nicht in die Lehre der absoluten Bewegung eindringen, als die so ge priesenen Entdeckungen der Kräfte darin herra 10
e: §. 210. Gravitation is the true and determinate Concept of material corporeality, which is thereby just as essentially divided into particular bodies, and has its appearing determinate being, the moment of external singularity, in motion, which is thereby immediately determined as a relation of several bodies. Universal gravitation must be acknowledged for itself as a profound thought, which constitutes an absolute foundation for mechanics, even though, grasped at first in the sphere of reflection, it drew attention and confidence to itself chiefly through the quantitative determination connected with it, and was to find its confirmation only in the experience followed up from the solar system down to the phenomenon of capillary tubes. — Moreover, gravitation immediately contradicts the law of inertia, for by virtue of the former matter strives out of itself toward the other. — In the Concept of gravity, as shown, the two moments themselves, of being-for-itself and of the continuity that sublates being-for-itself, are contained. These moments of the Concept now undergo the fate of being grasped as particular forces, corresponding to attractive and repulsive force, in closer determination as centripetal and centrifugal force, which, like gravity, are to act on the bodies, independently of one another and contingently to collide in a third, the body. Thereby what is profound in the thought of gravity is again reduced to nothing, and so long can Concept and reason not penetrate into the doctrine of absolute motion, as the so highly praised discoveries of forces prevail in it.

Noch größer aber wird fie, wenn ihrer im Verhältniſſe zur S< were erwähnt. wird; die Gravitation, die auch Attraction genannt wird, erſcheint dann als daſſelbe mit der Centripetalfraft, das Geſel für dieſe einzelne Kraft als ein Geſetz des Ganzen der Gravitation, und die Centrifugalkraft, die ein anderesmal wieder für ſchlecht- Hin weſentlich gilt," als etwas ganz überflüſſiges. — In obigem Schluſſe, welcher die unmittelbare Idee der Schwere enthält, ſie ſelbſt nemlich als den Begriff, welcher durch die Befonderheit.der Körper in die äuſſerliche „Realität der Bewegung tritt, iſt die vernünftige Identität und Untrennbarkeit dieſer drey Momente enthalten. =- Auch zeigt ſich in demſelben die Relativität der Bewegung, als ſie ſchlechthin nur im Syſteme mehrerer und zwar nach verſchiedener Beſtimmung zu einander im Verhältniß ſtehender Körper einen Sinn hatz welche verſchiedene Beſtim» mung ſich ſogleich ergeben wird. $. 214. Die beſondern Körper, in welchen die Schwere rea» liſirt iſt, haben zu Beſtimmungen ihrer unterſchiedenen Natur die Momente ihres Begriffs. Einer iſt alſo das allgemeine Centrum des Inſichſeyns. Dieſem Extreme ſteht die aufferfihfeyende, “centrumloſe Einzelnheit entgegen. Die beſondern aber ſind andere, die in der Beſtimmung des Auſſerſichſeyns ſtehen und als zugleich inſichſeyende auch Centra für ſich find, und ſich auf den erſten als auf ihre weſentliche Einheit beziehen; — eine Beziehung, die nicht eine Beziehung von Maſſe zu Maſſe; ſondern qualitativ iſt.
e: — If one attentively follows the quantitative determinations that have been found concerning laws of these two forces, the confusion that arises from that separation soon reveals itself. It becomes still greater, however, when they are mentioned in relation to gravity; gravitation, which is also called attraction, then appears as the same as the centripetal force, the law for this single force as a law of the whole of gravitation, and the centrifugal force, which at another time again counts as absolutely essential, as something quite superfluous. — In the above syllogism, which contains the immediate Idea of gravity, namely gravity itself as the Concept that, through the particularity of the bodies, enters into the external reality of motion, the rational identity and inseparability of these three moments is contained. — The relativity of motion also shows itself in it, in that motion has a meaning absolutely only in the system of several bodies standing in relationship to one another, and indeed according to different determination; which different determination will emerge immediately. §. 211. The particular bodies, in which gravity is realized, have as determinations of their differentiated nature the moments of their Concept. One of them, then, is the universal center of being-within-itself. Over against this extreme stands the centerless singularity that is outside itself. The particular ones, however, are others, which stand in the determination of being-outside-itself and, as at the same time being-within-themselves, are also centers for themselves, and relate themselves to the first as to their essential unity; — a relation that is not a relation of mass to mass, but is qualitative.

bekanntlich von Keppler entdeckt worden; — eine‘ Entdefung von unfterbiihem Ruhme. Bewier fen hat Keppler dieſelbe in dem Sinne, daß er für die empiriſchen Data ihren allgemeinen Ausdruck gefunden hat. (5. ı45), Es iſt ſeitdem zu einer allgemeinen Redensart geworben, daß Newton erſt die Beweiſe jener Gefege gefunden habe. Nicht leicht iſt ein Ruhm ungerechter von einem erſten Entdeer auf einen andern übergegangen. I< mache hier nur darauf aufmerkſam, daß im Grunde bereits von den Mathematikern zugeſtanden wird 1) daß die Newtoniſchen Formeln ſich aus den Keppleriſchen Geſetken ableiten laſſen, 2) daß der Newtoniſche Beweis von dem Saße, daß ein dem Gravitations- -. geſetze unterworfener Körper ſich in einer Ellipſe um den Centralkörper bewege, auf eine koniſche Section überhaupt geht; während der Hauptſatz der bewieſen werden ſollte, gerade darin beſteht, daß die Bahn eines ſolchen Körpers nicht ein Kreis oder ſonſt eine koniſche Section, ſondern allein die Ellipſe iſt. Die Bedingungen, welhe die Bahn des Körpers zu einem beſtimmten Kegelſchnitte machen, werden auf/eifen empiriſchen Umſtand, nemlich eine beſondere Lage des Körpers in einem beſtimmten Zeitpunkte, und die zufällige Stärke eines Sto ßes, den er urſprünglich erhalten haben ſollte, zurückgeführt. 3) daß das ' Newtoniſche Gefeg von der ſogenannten Kraft der [p. 148] Schwere gleichfalls nuraus 1 der Erfahrung durch Induction aufgezeigt ist. Bey näherer Betrachtung zeigt sich, daß das, was Keppler auf eine einfache und erhabene Weise, in der Form von Gesezen der himmlischen Bewegung ausgesprochen, 1 Newton in die begrifflose Reflexionsform von Kraft der Schwere umgewandelt hat. Die ganze Manier dieses sogenannten Beweisens stellt überhaupt ein verworrenes Gewebe dar, aus Linien der bloß geometrischen Construction, welchen eine physicalische Bedeutung von selbstständigen Kräften gegeben wird, und aus leeren Verstandesbegriffen von einer beschleunigenden Kraft, von Zeittheilchen, zu deren Anfang jene immer von neuem einwirken, einer Kraft der Träg heit, welchederen vorherige Wirkung fortseßen foll u. s. f. Ein vernünftiger Beweis über die quantitativen Bestimmungen der freyen Bewegung kann allein auf den Begriffsbestimmungen des Raums und der Zeit, der Momente, deren Verhältniß die Bewegung ist, beruhen. §. 213. 1 §. 214.
e: The laws of absolutely free motion were, as is well known, discovered by Kepler; — a discovery of immortal fame. Kepler has proved it in the sense that he found for the empirical data their universal expression. (§ 145) It has since become a common saying that Newton first found the proofs of those laws. Hardly ever has a fame passed more unjustly from a first discoverer to another. I merely call attention here to the fact that, at bottom, it is already conceded by mathematicians 1) that the Newtonian formulas can be derived from the Keplerian laws, 2) that the Newtonian proof of the proposition that a body subject to the law of gravitation moves in an ellipse around the central body applies to a conic section in general; whereas the main proposition that was to be proved consists precisely in this, that the orbit of such a body is not a circle or any other conic section, but alone the ellipse. The conditions that make the orbit of the body a determinate conic section are traced back to an empirical circumstance, namely a particular position of the body at a determinate point in time, and the contingent strength of an impact that it is supposed originally to have received. 3) that the Newtonian law of the so-called force of [p. 148] gravity is likewise shown only from experience through induction. — On closer consideration it turns out that what Kepler expressed in a simple and sublime manner, in the form of laws of the heavenly motion, Newton has transformed into the conceptless reflective form of force of gravity. The whole manner of this so-called proving presents, in general, a confused web, of lines of the merely geometrical construction, to which a physical meaning of independent forces is given, and of empty concepts of the understanding of an accelerating force, of time-particles, at the beginning of which those always act anew, of a force of inertia, which is to continue their previous effect, etc. — A rational proof concerning the quantitative determinations of free motion can rest solely on the determinations of the Concept of space and time, of the moments whose relationship is motion. §. 213. §. 214.

o: Die Trennung von dem unmittelbaren Zusammen. Hange, in welchem ein solcher Körper ruht, ist ein zufälliger Zustand, den er, wenn das äusserliche Hinderniß seines Zusammenhangs gehoben, durch den 1 Fall [p. 149] aufhebt, eine relativfreye Bewegung, indem jenes Entfernen dem Körper als unselbstständigem nicht zukommt, aber die Bewegung, wenn das Hinderniß entfernt wird, ihm immanent und eine Erscheinung seiner eigenen Schwere ist. Diese Bewegung geht für sich selbst in Ruhe über.
e: The separation from the immediate connection in which such a body rests is a contingent state, which it, when the external obstacle to its connection has been lifted, sublates through the fall [p. 149] — a relatively free motion, inasmuch as that removal does not belong to the body as a dependent one, but the motion, when the obstacle is removed, is immanent to it and an appearance of its own gravity. This motion passes over of itself into rest.

o: Die anziehende Kraft der Sonne z. B. gegen die Planeten oder der Erde gegen die ihr angehörigen und selbstständigen Körper, führt die schiefe Vorstellung mit sich, als ob sie eine dem Centralkörper inwohnende Activität wäre, und die in ihrer Sphäre befindlichen Körper sich nur passiv und äusserlich dagegen verhielten. - So wird auch die absolute Bewegung durch die Anwendung von Bestimmungen der gemeinen Mechanik als der todte Conflict von einer selbstständigen Tangentialkraft und einer eben so selbstständigen vom Mittelpunkt ausgehenden Kraft vorgestellt, vonwelchen der Körper passiv hin und hergezogen wäre. Das Galileische Geseß des Falles, daß die durchgelaufenen Räume sich wie die Quadrate der verflossenen Zeiten verhalten, zeigt gegen die abstracte gleichförmige Geschwindigkeit des todten Mechanismus, wo die Räume den Zeiten proportional sind, das Freywerden der Begriffsbestimmungen der Zeit und des Raumes, von denen jene als das negative Moment oder Princip des Eins die Bestimmung der Wurzel, dieser aber als das Aussereinanderseyn, und zwar ein, ohne eine andere Bestimmtheit als die der Wurzel, Aussersichkommen, die Bestimmung des Quadrats hat. In diesem Geseke bleiben beyde Momente noch in diesem Verhältnisse, weil die Freyheit der Bewegung im Falle, da sie auch bedingt ist, nur formell ist; in der absoluten Bewegung hingegen ist das Verhältniß in seiner Totalität, da sie die in sich zurückkehrende Bewegung ist. Weil das [p. 150] Gesek wesentlich Verhältniß ist, so sind Raum und Zeit in ihrem ursprünglichen Unterschiede gehalten; die dimensionslose Zeit kommt also nur zur formellen Identität mit sich, der Raum dagegen als das positive Aussereinander zur Dimension des Begriffs. Das Kepplerische Gesek ist daher ein Verhältniß des Würfels der Entfernungenzu den Quadraten der Zeiten; ein Gesek, das darum so groß 1 ist, weil es so einfach und unmittelbar die Ver nunft der Sache darstellt, da hingegen die Newtonische Formel, wodurch es in ein Gesek für die Kraft der Schwere verwandelt wird, nur die Verdrehung und Umkehrung der auf halbem Wege stehen bleibenden Reflexion zeigt. §. 215. Das Gesek die Trägheit ist zunächst von der Natur der Bewegung unselbstständiger Körper genommen, denen die Bewegung, weil sie die Differenz der Schwere nicht an ihnen selbst haben, aus
e: The attractive force of the sun, e.g., toward the planets, or of the earth toward the bodies belonging to it and independent, brings with it the skewed representation, as if it were an activity indwelling in the central body, and the bodies located in its sphere behaved only passively and externally toward it. — So too absolute motion, through the application of determinations of ordinary mechanics, is represented as the dead conflict of an independent tangential force and an equally independent force proceeding from the center, by which the body would be pulled passively hither and thither. — The Galilean law of fall, that the spaces traversed are related as the squares of the elapsed times, shows, in contrast with the abstract uniform velocity of dead mechanism, where the spaces are proportional to the times, the becoming free of the determinations of the Concept of time and of space, of which the former, as the negative moment or principle of the one, has the determination of the root, the latter, however, as being-outside-one-another, and indeed a coming-outside-itself without any other determinacy than that of the root, the determination of the square. In this law both moments still remain in this relationship, because the freedom of motion in fall, since it is also conditioned, is only formal; in absolute motion, on the other hand, the relationship is in its totality, since it is the motion returning into itself. Because the [p. 150] law is essentially a relationship, space and time are held in their original difference; the dimensionless time therefore comes only to the formal identity with itself, space, on the other hand, as the positive being-outside-one-another, to the dimension of the Concept. The Keplerian law is therefore a relationship of the cube of the distances to the squares of the times; — a law that is so great for this very reason, because it so simply and immediately presents the reason of the matter, whereas the Newtonian formula, by which it is transformed into a law for the force of gravity, shows only the distortion and inversion of the reflection that stops halfway. §. 215. The law of inertia is taken first of all from the nature of the motion of dependent bodies, to which motion, since they do not have the difference of gravity in themselves, is external.

o: serlich ist. Aber ebendarum ist die Ruhe ihnen im manent, nemlich die Identität mit dem ausser ihnen liegenden Centrum. Ihre Bewegung geht daher wesentlich in die Ruhe, aber nicht in absolute, sondern in den Druck, als Streben nach ihrem Centrum über, welches Streben, wenn es als ein str ebendes Bewegen angesehen werden soll, wenigstens die Veränderung jener äusserlichen Bewegung in dieses Strebenist, das die Natur des Körpers ausmacht. Das einzelne Hinderniß oder das allgemeine, die Reibung, ist zwar ein äusserliches, aber ein nothwendiges; es ist die Erscheinung jenes durch den Begriff desunselbstständigen Körpers gesekten Uebergangs. Eben dieß sindet auch in Ansehung des Pendels Statt, von dessen Bewegung gesagt zu werden pflegt, daß sie ohne Aufhören fort- * dauernwürde, wenn die Reibung entfernt werden könnte. Für sich drückt das Gesek der Trägheit nichts aus, als das Festhalten des Verstandes an den Abstractionen von Ruhe und Bewegung, daß nemlich die Ruhe nur Ruhe, die Bewegung nur Bewegung ist; der Uebergang dieser Abstractionen in einander, welcher der Begriffist, ist für den Verstand etwas Neusserliches. Dieses Gesek der. Trägheit, der Stoß, das Anziehen und andere Bestimmungen sind unstatthaft aus der gemeinen Mechas nick in die absolute übergetragen worden, in welcher die Bewegung vielmehr in ihrem freyen Begriffe ist. §. 216.
e: But precisely for this reason rest is immanent to them, namely the identity with the center lying outside them. Their motion therefore passes essentially into rest, but not into absolute rest, but into pressure, as striving toward their center, which striving, if it is to be regarded as a striving moving, is at least the alteration of that external motion into this striving, which constitutes the nature of the body. — The single obstacle or the universal one, friction, is indeed an external one, but a necessary one; it is the appearance of that transition posited by the Concept of the dependent body. — Precisely this also takes place with regard to the pendulum, of whose motion it is customary to say that it would continue without ceasing if friction could be removed. — Taken by itself, the law of inertia expresses nothing but the understanding's holding fast to the abstractions of rest and motion, namely that rest is only rest, motion only motion; the transition of these abstractions into one another, which is the Concept, is for the understanding something external. — This law of inertia, the impact, the attracting and other determinations have been transferred inadmissibly from ordinary mechanics into the absolute, in which motion is rather in its free Concept. §. 216.

o: DerUnterschied von Centralkörpern, und von unselbstständigen ist im Insichseyn der Schwere selbst, deren identische Natur ihre Eristenz ist. Der unselbstständige hat als das Aussersichseyn der mit sich identischen Schwere den Beginn des realen Unterschieds; er hat nur ein negatives Centrum der Schwere, einen Schwerpunkt sei = [p. 152] ner Masse; die Bestimmtheit seiner Bewegung ist nicht an und für sich, sondern tritt zu einem Factor zurück, zu dem die Masse der andere ist, so daß deren Größe sich vertauschen kann, und die Bewegung dieselbe bleibt. §. 217. Diese Neusserlichkeit des Bestimmtseyns macht die eigenthumliche Bestimmtheit der Materie aus; hiemit bleibt es nicht beym quantitativen Unterschiede stehen, sondern dieser ist wesentlich qualitativer, so daß die Bestimmtheit der Materie ihr Seyn ausmacht. * Die leere Abstraction einer formlosen Materie läßt einen bloß quantitativen Unterschied derselben zu, und sieht die fernere Bestimmtheit als eine ihr nicht wesentliche Form an. Schon die, Attractivund Repulsivkräfte, sollen äusserlich auf sie wirken. Da sie der aussersichsekende Begriff ist, so ist sie so sehr identisch mit der bestimmten Form, daß diese ihre eigenthümliche Natur ausmacht. B. 1 Elementarische Physik. §. 218.! Die Schwere, als in sich seyendes Wesen der Materie, nur innere Identität, geht, da ihr Begriff die wesentliche Neuserlichkeit ist, in die Manifestation des Wesens über. Als solche ist sie die Totalität der Reflexionsbestimmungen, aber dieselbe auseinandergeworfen, jede als eine besonders qualificirte Materie erscheinend, welche, als noch nicht zur Einzelnheit bestimmt, gestaltloses Element ist.
e: The difference between central bodies and dependent ones is in the being-within-itself of gravity itself, whose identical nature is its existence. The dependent one, as the being-outside-itself of the self-identical gravity, has the beginning of real difference; it has only a negative center of gravity, a point of gravity of its mass; [p. 152] the determinacy of its motion is not in and for itself, but recedes into a factor, to which the mass is the other, so that their magnitude can be interchanged and the motion remains the same. §. 217. This externality of being-determined makes up the peculiar determinacy of matter; thereby it does not stop at the quantitative difference, but this is essentially more qualitative, so that the determinacy of matter makes up its being. The empty abstraction of a formless matter admits a merely quantitative difference of it, and regards the further determinacy as a form not essential to it. Already the attractive and repulsive forces are supposed to act externally upon it. Since it is the Concept positing itself outside itself, it is so identical with the determinate form that this makes up its peculiar nature. B. §. 218. Gravity, as the essence of matter that is within itself, merely inner identity, passes over, since its Concept is the essential externality, into the manifestation of the essence. As such it is the totality of the determinations of reflection, but the same thrown asunder, each appearing as a particularly qualified matter, which, as not yet determined to singularity, is a shapeless element.

e: bundles of the same, of which a light restricted in its spreading is supposed to consist, belongs to the remaining barbarism of concepts that has become dominant in physics especially since Newton. — The inseparability of light, in its infinite extension, a real being-outside-one-another that remains identical with itself, can least of all be declared incomprehensible by the understanding, since its own principle is rather this abstract identity. — If astronomers have come to speak of heavenly appearances which, while they are being perceived by us, are said to have already occurred 500 years ago and more, one can in this, on the one hand, believe empirical appearances of the propagation of light, which hold in one sphere, to be transferred to another, where they have no significance, but on the other hand see a past become a present in the ideal manner of recollection. — According to the representation that from each point of a visible surface rays are sent out in all directions, and hence a material hemisphere of infinite dimension is formed from each, all these infinitely many hemispheres interpenetrate. Instead, however, of a condensed, confused mass having to arise through this between the eye and the object, and of the visibility to be explained having to produce, by virtue of this explanation, invisibility rather, this whole representation itself reduces itself rather to nullity, just as the representation of a concrete body that is supposed to consist of many matters, so that the others are located in the pores of the one, in which, conversely, the others themselves are lodged and circulate, — sublates, through this all-sided interpenetration, the assumption of the discrete materiality of the stuffs, and rather establishes a [p. 155] wholly ideal relationship. — The self-like nature of light, insofar as the natural things are enlivened by it, individualized and their opening-up is strengthened and held together, first comes to light in the individualization of matter, in that the at first abstract identity is only as the return and sublation of particularity, as the negative unity of singularity. §. 221. Light relates itself, as universal identity, first of all in this determination of diversity or of the understanding of the moments of the totality, to concrete matter as something external and other, as to a dark; this contact and external clouding of the one by the other is color.

e: According to the well-known Newtonian theory, white, i.e., colorless light, consists of five or of seven colors; — for the theory itself does not know this exactly. — On the barbarism, first of all, of the representation that with light too recourse has been had to the worst form of reflection, composition, and that the bright is here supposed even to consist of seven darknesses, just as one could let clear water consist of seven earths, one can not express oneself strongly enough; as well as, further, on the clumsiness, insipidity, indeed even dishonesty of the Newtonian observing and experimenting; — then on the equally bad constitution of the concluding, inferring and proving from those impure empirical data; — further on the blindness of the parroting now carried on for nearly a century and a half, as well as on the ignorance of these parrots who defend that simple-minded representation, [p. 156] finally, in particular, about the thoughtlessness with which a number of the immediate consequences of that theory (e.g., the impossibility of achromatic telescopes) have been given up and yet the theory itself is maintained; — lastly, about the blindness of the prejudice that it rests on something mathematical, and as if the measurements, in part themselves false and one-sided, as well as the quantitative determinations brought into the inferences, furnished any ground for the theory and the nature of the matter itself. — A principal reason why the Goethean illumination of this darkness in light, as clear as it is thorough and learned, has not met with a more effective reception is, without doubt, this: because the thoughtlessness and simple-mindedness, which one ought to admit, are altogether too great. — Instead of these absurd representations having diminished, they have in the most recent times, following Malus's discoveries, been further increased by a polarization of light, and even by the quadrangularity of the sun's rays, by a left-rotating motion of the red and a right-rotating one of the blue rays. Such instances of simple-mindedness justify themselves by the privilege of physics to the so-called hypotheses; but one permits oneself no instances of simple-mindedness in jest, much less should one put forward such things for hypotheses that are not even supposed to be a jest. §. 222. Light makes up the determinate being or the physical meaning of the body of abstract centrality, which as light-body is real.

e: These two bodies also have, in the system of gravity, as relative central bodies, their more determinate meaning, which has the same Concept at its ground as their physical one does, and which can be noted here. — They do not rotate about their axis. The body of rigidity, as of formal being-for-itself, which is the independence involved in opposition and therefore not individuality, is for this reason serving and the satellite of another, in which it has its axis. The body of dissolution, the opposite of rigidity, is in its behavior erratic, and, in its eccentric orbit as in its physical determinate being, presents contingency; so that it has been conjectured of these bodies that the proximity of a great planet could alter their orbit; — they show themselves as a superficial concretion, which may just as contingently disperse again. — The moon has no atmosphere, and thereby lacks the meteorological process. It shows only high mountains and craters, and the inflammation of this rigidity within itself; the shape of a crystal, which Heim (one of the few ingenious geognosts) has pointed out as the original one of the merely rigid earth. — The comet appears [p. 158] as a formal process, a restless mass of vapor; none has shown anything rigid, a nucleus. Against the representation of the ancients, that comets are mere meteors, astronomers in the most recent times, however, no longer act so aloof and superior as formerly. As yet only the return of a single one has been observed; others were expected according to calculation, but did not come. — The conjecture put forward by astronomers also points to this, that they could in time give up the hitherto formal view of the appearance of the comets, contingent in relation to the whole of the system and emerging athwart and across it, and grasp the thought that the other bodies of the same defend themselves against them, i.e., behave as necessary organic moments, so that they would also put themselves in a position to offer better grounds of consolation than hitherto against the dangers feared from the comet. — §. 224.

e: One is accustomed to hold the sun and the stars to be more excellent natures than the planets, because the first elevation of reflection above sensuous perception takes the abstract for the highest as against the singular, which is not yet comprehended. — The name wandering stars has arisen for the bodies of individuality from the immediate view of their motion; in and for itself, however, this is, as axial rotation about itself and at the same time motion [p. 159] around a central body the most concrete, expression of vitality, and for that reason just as much more excellent than the rest of the center of the system as than the serving and erratic motion of the lunar and cometary bodies. Likewise the light-nature of the central body is the abstract identity, whose truth, as that of thinking, is in the concrete Idea, in individuality. — As for the series of the planets, astronomy has discovered, concerning their nearest determinacy, the distance, as yet no actual law, much less anything rational. What I attempted on this in an earlier dissertation I can no longer regard as satisfactory. — Likewise the attempts in the philosophy of nature to show the rationality of the series in the physical constitution can so far be regarded only as beginnings of finding the points of view that matter. — What is irrational is to lay the thought of contingency at the ground of this, and, e.g., in Kepler's thought of grasping the arrangement of the solar system according to the laws of musical harmony, to see only an aberration of the imagination, and not to esteem highly the deep belief that reason is in this system; — a belief that was the sole ground of his brilliant discoveries. The wholly clumsy and erroneous application of the numerical relationships of tones which Newton made to colors has, on the other hand, retained renown and credence. §. 225.

e: §. 229. §. 230. The individual identity, under which the differing elements, and their diversity against one another and against their unity, are bound, is a dialectic that makes up the physical life of the earth, the meteorological process; the elements, as dependent moments, have in it their subsistence only to the same extent as they are produced in it. Just as the determinations of ordinary mechanics and of the independent bodies are applied to absolute mechanics and the free central bodies, so the finite physics of the individuated individual bodies is taken for the same as the free, independent physics of the earth-process is. It is held to be precisely the triumph of science to recognize again and demonstrate in the universal process of the earth the same determinations that show themselves in the external and dependent processes of individuated physical corporeality. The demonstration of this likeness is effected by the determinations being made, through abstraction from their peculiar differences and conditions, into superficial universalities, such as attraction, — forces and laws, in which the particular, the concrete Concept and the conditions are lacking, and were then partly regarded as an external stuff entering in, partly also, by analogy, added by invention.

What goes beyond these and is only assumed is a matter of thinking. It does not occur to physics, however, that it has thoughts; which is true in a double sense, and here in the third, that the pores are mere inventions. — An immediate example of a peculiar specification of gravity is the appearance that an iron bar poised in equilibrium on its point of support, [p. 166] as it is magnetized, loses its equilibrium and now shows itself heavier at the one pole than at the other. — The propositions that physics presupposes in its way of representing density are: 1) that an equal number of equally large material parts are equally heavy; — thus one remains stuck at the formal identity of gravity. 2) The measure of the number of the parts is the weight, but 3) also space, so that what is of equal weight also takes up equal space; if therefore 4) equal weights nevertheless appear in a different volume, then, by the assumption of pores, the equality of the space that is filled is maintained. — Kant has already opposed intensity to the quantitative determination of number, and put in the place of more parts in equal space the equal number but of a stronger degree of space-filling, and thereby given the origin to a so-called dynamical physics. — At least the determination of the intensive quantum would have as much right as that of the extensive; but this difference (§ 56) is empty and null in itself. e: Magnetism is one of the determinations that had to present themselves above all when thought surmised itself in determinate nature, and conceived the idea of a philosophy of nature. For the magnet presents, in a simple, naive manner, the nature of the Concept. The poles are not particular things; they do not have the sensuous, mechanical reality, but an ideal one; the point of indifference, in which they have their substance, is the unity in which they are only as determinations of the Concept, and polarity is an opposition only of such moments. The appearances that allow magnetism to be regarded as something merely particular are only ever the same determinations again and again, not different properties that could give data for a description. — That the single magnetic needle directs itself toward the north and thereby, at one and the same time, toward the south, is appearance of the universal earth-magnetism; the same, that of [p. 168] two such empirical magnets the like-named poles repel one another and the unlike-named attract one another; which is precisely magnetism itself, that the like, the indifferent, dirempts itself and opposes itself into extremes, and the unlike, the different, posits its indifference; one has even called the unlike-named poles friendly, the like-named, however, hostile. — That all bodies, however, are magnetic has a skewed double meaning; the correct one is that every real shape, not merely brittle shape, contains this Concept; the incorrect one, however, that all bodies also have in themselves this principle in its strict abstraction, as it is as magnetism. To want to show a form of the Concept as present in nature by claiming that it should exist universally in the determinacy in which it is as an abstraction would be an unphilosophical thought. Nature is rather the Idea in the element of being-outside-one-another, so that it, just as the understanding does, holds the moments of the Concept fast scattered and presents them in reality, but in the higher organic things unites the highest concretion of the different forms of the Concept in one. §. 239. e: Between the two properly shapeless extremes, punctual brittleness and the fluidity that forms itself into a sphere, falls the real shape in the unification [p. 169] of those extremes, the magnetism that has passed over into total corporeality, cohesion. §. 241. Common cohesion concerns merely the single moment of the quantitative strength of the coherence of the parts of a body. Concrete cohesion is immanent form and determinacy of this coherence, and comprises the external crystallizations and the fracture shapes or core shapes, the internal crystallization that shows itself going right through. §. 242. Through external crystallization the individual body is closed off as a singular against others, and is capable of a mechanical process with them. As internally formed, it specifies this process against its behavior as a mere universal mass; in elasticity, hardness, softness, toughness, ductility, shatterability, it thus obtains its individual determinacy in the resistance to external force. §. 243. But just as density is the simple determinacy only at first, as the relationship of volume to mass, so cohesion is this simplicity as the self-like of individuality. The self-preservation of the body in the shaking by mechanical force is therefore also an emergence of its individual pure ideality, of its peculiar motion within itself through its whole cohesion; the specific determination of its ideal being-asunder within itself through its self-like time. This trembling, which the body lets appear as its own and indeed specified ideality, in face of real force and external alteration, is sound.

e: In the case of the old, universal thought that every body consists of the four elements, or of the more recent Paracelsian one that it consists of mercury or fluidity, sulfur or oil, and salt, and of many other thoughts of this kind, the refutation has been easy in the first place, in that one [p. 171] wanted to understand by those names the individual empirical stuffs that are first of all designated by such names. e: As is well known, the earlier difference, bound to a determinate sensuous existence, between glass- and resin-electricity has been idealized, through completed empirical science, into the difference of thought between positive and negative electricity; — a remarkable example of how empirical science, which at first wants to grasp and hold fast the universal in sensuous form, sublates itself. — If much has been said in recent times about the polarization of light, then [p. 173] this expression would have been reserved with greater right for electricity than for Malus’s phenomena, in which transparent media, reflecting surfaces and the different positions of these toward one another, as well as a determinate angle of incidence of the light, are so many other different circumstances that show no difference in the light itself, but only in its shining. — The conditions under which positive and negative electricity emerge, the smoother or duller surface, e.g., a breath, and so on, prove the superficiality of the electrical process and how little the concrete physical nature of the body enters into it. In just the same way the faint coloring of the two electrical lights, smell, taste, show only the beginning of a corporeality at the abstract self of light, in which the process remains. The negativity that is the sublation of the opposed tension is chiefly a shock; — the self that posits itself as identical with itself remains, even as such, within the ideal sphere of space and time and mechanism. Light has hardly a beginning of materializing itself into heat, and the ignition that can arise from the so-called discharge is (Berthollet Statique Chimique Ière Partie, Sect. III. not. XI.) more a direct effect of the shaking than the consequence of a realization of light into fire. — Galvanism is the electrical process made more permanent; it has permanence as the contact of two different, non-brittle bodies, which, for the sake of their fluid nature (the so-called electrical conductivity of the metals), give immediate determinate being, against one another, to their whole difference, and, for the sake of their solidity and of the [p. 174] superficiality of this relation, maintain themselves and their tension against one another. The galvanic process comes about only through this particular peculiarity of bodies of a more concrete and more corporeal nature, and makes the transition to the chemical process. §. 250. The individuality of the body is the negative unity of the Concept, which is absolutely not an immediate and unmoved universal, but one that posits itself only through the mediation of the process; the body is therefore product, and its shape a presupposition by which, rather, the end into which it passes over is presupposed. — Particularization, however, does not remain standing at the merely inert diversity and opposition, only as tension and difference of pure selfhood, but, since the particular properties are only the reality of this simple Concept, the body of their soul, of light, the whole corporeality enters into the tension and the process, which is the formation of the individual body, individuation; — the chemical process. §. 251.

Immediate according to the Concept is the particularized body, insofar as its properties or matters have been unified into simple determination and have become equal to the simplicity of specified gravity, of density. The middle, through which the Concept, which is in itself the unity of both and the essence of each, joins together these compact differences with its reality, — or posits the difference of each of the two as one with the difference of the other, and thereby becomes real as totality of its Concept, is first of all, over against the immediate solidity of the extremes, the abstract neutrality, the element of water. e: bodies alongside one another; just as chaotically abstract and more real processes are placed on the same level. If a scientific form is to enter into this medley, every product is to be determined according to the stage of the process from which it essentially emerges and which gives it its peculiar significance; and it is just as essential to distinguish the stages of abstraction or reality of the process. Animal and vegetable substances belong in any case to an entirely different order, and their nature can so little be comprehended from the chemical process that they are rather destroyed by it, and only the path of their death is grasped therein. These substances, however, should serve most of all to counteract the metaphysics that is dominant in chemistry as in physics, namely the thoughts, or rather wild representations, of the unalterability of the stuffs, of their composition and of consisting of them. But we see it generally admitted that the chemical stuffs lose in union the properties they show in separation, and yet see the representation hold good that without the properties they are the same things as they are with them, and as things with these properties are not first products of the process. — An important step toward the simplification of the particularities in the elective affinities has been made through the law found by Richter and Guyton Morveau, that neutral compounds undergo no alteration in respect of the state of saturation when they are mixed through solution and the acids exchange their bases with one another. Connected with this is the scale of the quantities of acids [p. 179] and alkalis, according to which each single acid has a particular relationship, for its saturation, to that alkaline one, yet in such a way that for every other acid, whose quantitative unity is different only from that of the rest, the alkalis now have among themselves the same relationship to their saturation as to the rest of the acids, so that the acids too show among themselves a constant relationship toward every different alkaline one. — Since the chemical process, moreover, has its determination in the Concept, the empirical conditions of a particular form of it, as with electricity, are not such firm sensuous determinations and not such abstract moments as one imagines, e.g., in the case of elective affinity; Berthollet, in his celebrated work Statique chimique, has compiled and investigated the circumstances that bring about an alteration in the results of chemical action — results that are supposed to flow only from conditions of affinity, which one regards as constant and firmly determined laws; he says that the superficiality that science obtains through these explanations is regarded chiefly as progress on its part. §. 258.

e: The chemical process is indeed, in general, life, whereby the individual body is sublated and produced in its immediacy, so that the Concept no longer remains inner necessity, but comes to appearance. But it comes also only to this, not to objectivity. — This process is a finite and transitory one, because the single body is immediate individuality, and so a limited particularity, and the process thereby has immediate and contingent conditions. In the neutral [p. 180] the difference and the fire are extinguished; it does not kindle itself within itself to disunion; just as the different exists at first in indifferent independence, does not stand for itself in relation with one another, nor inspirit itself. The chemical phenomena — that, e.g., in the process an oxide is reduced to a lower degree of oxidation, at which it can combine with the acting acid, and a part of it, on the other hand, is more strongly oxidized — induce chemists to apply the determination of purposiveness in the explanation; — in which, thereby, the self-determination of the Concept in realization lies. §. 259. In the process the body shows, both in its coming-to-be and in its passing-away, the transience of its immediate individuality, and presents itself as a moment of the universal one; in the latter the Concept has its reality corresponding to it, a concrete universality that has come to be out of particularization, which thus contains within itself the conditions and moments of the total syllogism that fall asunder in the immediate process of chemism; — the organism. §. 260.

e: The real totality of the individual body, in that it has made its particularity into a product and has just as much sublated it, has thereby raised itself into the first ideality of nature, so that, however, it has become a filled one, and essentially self-like and subjective. The Idea has thus come to existence, at first to the immediate one, to life. This is a) as shape, [p. 181] the universal image of life; the geological organism; b) as particular or formal subjectivity, the vegetable one, c) as singular concrete subjectivity, animal nature. A. §. 261. The universal system of individual bodies is the earth, which in the chemical process has, at first, its abstract individuality in particularization, but, as totality of the same, is the infinite relation to itself, a universal process kindling itself, — the immediate subject and product of the same. But as the immediate totality that the subjective totality has presupposed to itself, the earth-body is only the shape of the organism. §. 262. The members of this organism therefore do not contain the universality of the process within themselves; they are the particular individuals, and make up a system, whose formations present themselves as members of the unfolding of an underlying Idea, whose formative process is a past one. §. 263.

e: The powers of this process, which nature leaves behind beyond the earth as independent entities, are the connection and the position of the earth in the solar system, its solar, lunar and cometary life, the inclination of its axis to the orbit, and the magnetic axis. In closer relation to these axes and their polarization stands the distribution of sea and land, whose continuous extension in the north, [p. 182] the division and pointed narrowing of the parts toward the south, the further separation into an old and a new world, and the subsequent distribution of the former into the parts of the world, differing from one another, and from the new world, through their physical, organic and anthropological character, to which a still younger and more immature one attaches itself; — the mountain ranges, etc. §. 264. The physical organization indicates a graded progression from the granitic mountain core, which presents a triad of determinations within itself, of which the other formations are partly transitions and modifications, in which its totality remains the existing foundation, only as one more unequal and more formless within itself, partly a stepping-asunder of its moments into more determinate difference and into more abstract mineral moments, the metals and the oryctognostic objects in general, until they lose themselves in mechanical layerings and in alluvial deposits lacking immanent configuration. §. 265. This crystal of life, the dead-lying organism of the earth, which has its Concept in the sidereal connection, but its process as a presupposed past, is the immediate subject of the meteorological process, the subject which is, as this organized whole, in its complete determinacy. In this objective subject the previously elemental process is now the objective and individual one, — the sublation of that immediacy, whereby the universal individuality now becomes for itself and life becomes the living being, i.e., actual. The first actual vitality that the fertile earth brings forth is vegetable nature.

e: B. §. 266. The universality of life and its singularity are immediately identical in immediate vitality. The process of articulation and self-preservation of the vegetable subject is therefore a coming-outside-itself, and a falling apart into several individuals, for which the one whole individual is more the mere soil than their subjective unity. Furthermore, for that reason the difference of the organic parts is only a superficial metamorphosis, and the one can easily pass over into the function of the other. §. 267. The process of configuration and of reproduction of the single individual coincides in this way with the process of the genus; and because the self-like universality, the subjective one of individuality, is not separated from the real particularization but is merely sunk into it, the plant has no motion from its place, nor an interrupting intussusception, but a continuously flowing nourishment; it does not relate itself to an individualized inorganic, but to the universal elements; nor is it capable of feeling and of animal heat. §. 268.

e: Insofar, however, as life is essentially the Concept, which realizes itself only through self-disunion and re-uniting, the processes of the plant also fall asunder. 1) Its inner process of configuration is, however, partly, as positive, only immediate transformation of the inflows of nourishment into the specific nature of the plant species. Partly this process is, as mediation, for the sake of its [p. 184] essential simplicity, the disunion, on the one hand into the abstract universal of the individuality inseparable within itself, as into the negative of vitality, lignification; on the other hand, however, as the side of singularity and vitality, immediately the process that specifies itself outward. §. 269. §. 270. But because the reproduction of the vegetable individual as a singular one is not the subjective return into itself, a feeling of self, but, inwardly, lignification, the production of the plant’s self therewith goes outward. It gives birth to its light out in the blossom, in which the neutral, green color is determined to a specific clouding, or else the light is produced pure of the dark, as white color. §. 271. In that the plant thus offers up its self in sacrifice, this externalization is at the same time the Concept realized through the process, the plant that has produced itself as a whole, but has therein stepped over against itself. This highest point is therefore the beginning of a sexual difference and the indication of the process of the genus.

e: The animal has contingent self-motion, because its subjectivity, like light and fire, an ideality wrested from gravity, — is a free time, which, as at the same time withdrawn from real externality, determines itself, according to inner contingency, even to place. Connected with this is that the animal has voice, in that its subjectivity, as being in and for itself, is the dominion of the abstract ideality of time and space, and presents its [p. 186] self-motion as the ideal, inner individuality of a free trembling within itself; — animal heat, as the continuing process of dissolution of cohesion in the continuing preservation of shape; — interrupted intussusception, — but above all feeling, as the individuality that is immediately universal to itself in determinacy and distinguishes itself from it as actual. §. 275. The animal organism is, as living universality, the Concept, which courses through its three determinations, each of which is the same total identity of the substantial unity and at the same time, for itself as determination of form, the passing over into the others, so that from the same the totality results; only as this self-reproducing, not as something that is, is the living being. §. 276. It is therefore α) its simple, universal being-within-itself in its externality, whereby the actual determinacy is received immediately as particularity into the universal, and this thereby is undivided identity of the subject with itself in that; — sensibility; — β) particularity, as excitability from without and the reaction, coming from the receiving subject, against it outward. — irritability; — γ) the unity of these moments, the negative return through the relationship of externality to itself, and thereby generation and positing of itself as a singular one, — reproduction; inwardly the reality and foundation of the former moments, and articulation and armament outwardly. §. 277.

e: These three moments of the Concept have their reality in the three systems, the nerve-, blood- [p. 187] and digestive system, of which the first turns itself in the systems of the bones and of the sense organs, the second in the lung and the muscles, outward on two sides; the digestive system, however, as glandular system with skin and cellular tissue, is an immediate, vegetative reproduction, but in the system of the viscera proper the mediating one. The animal is thereby divided for itself into the centers of three systems, (insectum) head, chest and abdomen, whereas the extremities, for mechanical motion and grasping, make up the moment of the singularity that posits itself as distinguished outwardly. §. 278. The Idea of the living being is the exhibited unity of the Concept with its reality; but it is, as opposition of that subjectivity and objectivity, essentially only as process, — as motion of the abstract relation of the living being to itself, which dirempts itself into particularity, and as return into itself is the negative unity of subjectivity and totality. Each of these moments, however, as a concrete moment of vitality, is itself process, and the whole is the unity of three processes. §. 279.

e: — When finite reason is spoken of, it proves precisely thereby that it is infinite, in that it determines itself as finite; for negation is finitude, lack only for that which is the being-sublated of it, the infinite relation to itself. — Thoughtlessness, however, stays at the abstraction of the limitation, and in life, where the Concept itself enters into existence, it likewise does not grasp it, but holds to determinations of representation, such as drive, instinct, need, etc. — That for the organism the determination of being excited by external potencies has taken the place of the acting-upon by external causes is an important step in the true representation of it. — Idealism begins in this: that in general nothing can have a positive relation to the living being whose possibility this would not be in and for itself, i.e., which would not be determined through the Concept, thus absolutely immanent to the subject. But as unphilosophical as any scientific brew of determinations of reflection is the introduction of such formal and material relationships in the theory of excitation, as have long passed for philosophical; e.g., the wholly abstract opposition of receptivity and capacity for effect, which as factors are supposed to stand to one another in inverse ratio of magnitude, whereby all difference to be grasped in the organism has fallen into the formalism of merely quantitative diversity, heightening and diminution, strengthening and weakening, i.e., into the highest possible conceptlessness. A theory of medicine that is built on these barren determinations of the understanding is completed with half a dozen [p. 191] propositions, and it is no wonder if it found rapid diffusion and many adherents. The occasion for this aberration of philosophy, with which nature had only just begun to make friends, lay in the fundamental error that, after the absolute had been determined as the absolute indifference of the subjective and the objective, all determination was now supposed to be only a quantitative difference. The absolute form, the Concept, and vitality have rather the qualitative difference, consuming itself within itself, alone as its soul. Because this true infinite negativity had not been cognized, it was thought that the absolute identity of life, as in Spinoza the attributes and modes occur in an external understanding, could not be held fast without making the difference into a merely external one of reflection; whereby life lacks the springing point of selfhood, the principle of self-motion, diremption of itself, singularity in general. — To be held entirely unphilosophical and crudely sensuous, further, is the procedure that wanted to give formal determinations a real meaning, and in place of determinations of the Concept even put carbon and nitrogen, oxygen and hydrogen, and determined the previously intensive difference, now, as the more or less of the one and the other stuff, but the effective and positive relationship of the external stimuli as an adding of a lacking stuff; — e.g., in an asthenia, — a nervous fever, nitrogen is said to have the upper hand in the organism, because the brain and the nerve in general are supposed to be the potentiated nitrogen, since chemical analysis shows it as the principal constituent of these organic formations; the addition of carbon is said to be hereby [p. 192] indicated, in order to restore the equilibrium of these stuffs, health. The remedies that have proved effective against nervous fever in an empirical manner are, for this very reason, regarded as belonging to the side of carbon, and such a superficial putting together and opining is passed off as construction and proving. — The crudity consists in this, that the external caput mortuum, the dead stuff, into which chemistry has killed a deadened life for the second time, is taken for the essence of a living organ, indeed for its Concept. This latter then grounds the so highly convenient formalism of using such sensuous materials as the chemical stuffs, further relationships that belong to the sphere of inorganic nature, such as the north and south polarity of magnetism, or the differences of this itself and of the electrical moment, instead of determinations of the Concept, and of comprehending and developing the natural universe in such a way that onto the spheres and differences that it presents, such a ready-made schema of north- and south-, west- and east-polarity, or whatever else it may be, is externally attached. A great multiplicity of forms is possible here, since it remains optional to adopt for the schema the determinations of the totality, as they appear in the chemical sphere, e.g., oxygen, hydrogen, etc., and to transfer them to magnetism, mechanism, vegetation, animality, etc., or else to take magnetism, electricity, the masculine and the feminine, contraction and expansion, etc., in general to reach for oppositions of any other sphere and to use them in the rest.

e: §. 283. Need and excitation are directed to the relationship of the universal and particular mechanism, (sleeping and waking), to the process with air, (respiratory and cutaneous process), with water, (thirst) and with individualized earth, namely particular formations of it (hunger, § 275). Life, the subject of these moments of the totality, tenses itself within itself as Concept and into the moments as a reality external to it, and is the continuing conflict in which it overcomes this externality. Because the animal, as essentially a singular, can do this only in the singular, this objectification of itself is not adequate to its Concept, and therefore continually goes back out of satisfaction into the state of need. §. 284. The mechanical mastering of the external Object is only the beginning of the uniting of it with the animal living being. Since this is thereby a subject, the simple negativity of the punctual one, assimilation can be of neither a mechanical nor, just as little, of a chemical nature, since in these processes the stuffs as well as the conditions and the activity remain external to one another, and lack the living absolute unity. §. 285.

e: It is, first, because the living being is the universal power over its external nature opposed to it, the immediate going-together of what is taken up inwardly with animality; an infection with this and simple transformation (§ 278). Second, since the power of the living being is the relation to itself through mediation, assimilation is digestion; — opposition of the subject against [p. 194] its immediate assimilating, so that the former, as negative, excites itself against it, and appears as the process of opposition, process of the animal water (of the gastric and pancreatic juice, of animal lymph in general) and of the animal fire (of the bile, in which the being-turned-back-into-itself of the organism, from its concentration, which it has in the spleen, is determined to being-for-itself and to active consumption). §. 286. This animal excitation is at first turned against the external potency, which, however, through the infection (§ 277) has been placed immediately on the side of the organism. But that excitation, as the opposition and the being-for-itself of the process against the universality and simple relation of the living being to itself, likewise has the determination of externality. Both together, appearing at first on the side of the subject as means, therefore actually constitute the Object and the negative against the organism, which it has to overcome and digest. §. 287. This inversion of the view is the reflection of the organism into itself, the negation of its own negativity or outwardly directed activity. As natural being, the singularity that it attains herein closes together with its universality as disjunctive in such a way that it, on the one hand, excretes from itself the first negation, the externality of the Object and its own activity, and, on the other hand, as immediately identical with this, has reproduced for itself its negation in this means; in that the process going outward is thus transformed out of itself and has passed over into the first formal elements of reproduction.

e: The main moment in digestion is the immediate effect of life, as the power over its inorganic Object, which it opposes to itself, and presupposes as its exciting stimulus only and insofar as it is in itself identical with it. This effect is infection and immediate transformation. Spallanzani’s and other experiments, and recent physiology, have proved, also in an empirical manner, and shown in accordance with the Concept, this immediacy, with which the living being as universal, without further mediation, through its mere contact and taking up of the foodstuff into its heat and sphere in general, continues itself into the same, against the mediation represented as a mechanical, fictitious sorting out and separating off of already homogeneous, usable parts, as well as against the mediation represented as a chemical process. The investigations, on the other hand, of the mediating actions have not yielded more determinate moments of this transformation (such as a series of fermentations presents itself, e.g., in vegetable stuffs); on the contrary they have shown, e.g., that already from the stomach onward much passes over into the mass of the juices without having had to go through the remaining stages of mediation, that the pancreatic juice is nothing further than saliva, and the pancreas can very well be dispensed with, etc. The last product, the chyle, which the thoracic duct takes up and pours into the blood, is the same lymph that each single viscus and organ excretes, that the skin and the lymphatic system everywhere obtain in the immediate process of transformation, and which is everywhere already prepared. The lowly animal organizations, which anyway are nothing but a lymph coagulated into a membranous point or little tube — a simple intestinal canal — do not go [p. 196] beyond this immediate transformation. The mediated digestive process, in the higher animal organizations, is, with regard to its peculiar product, just such a superfluity as, in plants, their seed-production mediated through so-called sexual difference. — The faeces show, especially in children, in whom the increase of matter nevertheless stands out most, frequently the greatest part of the foodstuffs unchanged, mixed chiefly with animal stuffs, the bile, phosphorus and the like, and as the principal effect of the organism, to overcome and remove its own productions. — The syllogism of the organism is therefore not the syllogism of external purposiveness, because it does not stop at directing its activity and form against the external Object, but makes this process itself, which because of its externality is on the point of becoming mechanical and chemical, into the Object, and, since it is nature, in the coming together of itself therein with itself, is disjunctive activity, which removes this process from itself, abstracts from its anger against the Object, this one-sided subjectivity, and thereby becomes for itself what it is in itself, — identity of its Concept and its reality, — thus finds the end and product of its activity as that which it already is from the beginning and originally. Hereby satisfaction is rational; the process going into external difference turns over into the process of the organism with itself, and the result is not the mere production of a means, but of the end.
