Through the process with the external nature the animal gives to the certainty of itself, to its subjective Concept, truth, objectivity, as singular individual; and is production of itself as much as self-preservation, or reproduction as production of its first Concept. Thereby the latter goes together with itself, and is as concrete universal, genus. The disjunction of the singularity that finds itself in the genus is the sexual difference, the relation of the subject to an Object that is itself such a subject. §. 289. This relation is drive; the singular as such is not adequate to its genus; nor does this adequacy fall into an external reflection; the individual, in its limitation of the genus, is at the same time the genus’s identical relation to itself in one unity; it thus has the feeling of this lack and is in natural difference of sex. §. 290. §. 291. e: The Concept of the animal has the Concept itself as its essence, because it is the actuality of the Idea of life. The nature of its universality makes it possible that it has a simpler and more developed determinate being, as well as one more or less corresponding to it. From determinate being itself, therefore, the Concept cannot be grasped in its determinacy. The classes in which it appears developed and completely presented in its moments appear as a particular determinate being against the rest, and also in those it can have a bad determinate being. But whether determinate being is bad, to this judgment the Concept is already presupposed. If, as is usual, determinate being was presupposed in order to cognize from it the nature of the animal and its essential determinations, or the essential organs of a class, then it comes [p. 199] on this empirical path to no firm determination, and all particular properties show themselves also in such a way that they can be lacking; e.g., the acephala have been cited as an instance that the human being could live even without a brain. — In zoology, as in the natural sciences in general, it has been more a matter of finding secure and simple marks for subjective cognition. Only since this end of so-called artificial systems has been lost sight of more in the cognition of animals has a larger view opened up, and among the empirical sciences there is hardly one that in recent times has gained such great expansions — not preeminently in the mass of observations, for no science has lacked that, but in respect of its material having worked itself toward rationality — as zoology, through its auxiliary science, comparative anatomy. Partly, in the individual formations, the habitus, as a connection determining the construction of all parts, has been made the main matter, so that the great founder of this science, Cuvier, could boast of being able to cognize the essential nature of the whole animal from a single bone. Partly the universal type of the animal has been followed through the various formations, however imperfect and disparate they appear, and in the scarcely beginning indication, as well as in the intermixture of organs and functions, their significance has been recognized, and by this very means it has been raised above and out of particularity into its universality. A main aspect of this consideration is the cognition of how nature forms this organism onto, and fits it snugly to, the particular element into which it throws it, to climate, circle of nourishment, in general to the world in [p. 200] which it is absorbed (which can also be a single plant genus or other animal genus). — It is the immediacy of the Idea of life that the Concept, although it alone is that which is determined in and for itself, does not as such exist in life, its determinate being therefore submits itself to the manifold conditions and circumstances of external nature, and can appear in the most meager forms, and the fertility of the earth lets it sprout everywhere. The animal world can therefore, almost less than the other spheres of nature, present a rational system of organization independent in itself, adhere to the forms that would be determined by the Concept, and preserve them against the imperfection and intermixture of conditions from mingling, stunting and transitions. — This weakness of the Concept, which in the animal does not exist in its firm, independent freedom, also subjects the existing genus entirely to the changes of the external universal life of nature, whose alternation it lives through along with it, and which in its singular existence is a continual violence against the single animal. Animal life therefore shows itself in general as a sick one; as also its feeling, as an insecure, anxious, and unhappy one. §. 293. The single organism can, because of the externality of its determinate being, also become non-corresponding to its determination. It finds itself in the state of disease, insofar as one of its systems or organs, excited into conflict with an inorganic potency, establishes itself for itself and persists in its particular activity against the activity of the whole, whose fluidity and process passing through all the moments is thereby inhibited.

e: §. 294. The peculiar appearance of disease is therefore that the identity of the whole organic Concept presents itself as successive course of the vital motion through its different moments, sensibility, irritability and reproduction, as fever, which, against the isolated activity, as the course of the totality, is just as much the attempt at and the beginning of healing. §. 295. The remedy excites the organism to remove the inorganic potency with which the activity of the single organ or system is entangled and thereby isolated, — but essentially to sublate the excitation in which the formal activity of the whole is fixed, and to restore fluidity into the whole. The remedy effects this by being a stimulus, but one still harder to assimilate and to overcome, against which the organism is compelled to summon up its whole force. In that it thus directs itself against something external, it has stepped out of the limitedness that had become identical with it, in which it had been caught up.

Jene innere Allgemeinheit ist daher gegen diese Wirklichkeit eine negative Macht, von welcher es Gewalt leidet und untergeht, weil sein Daseyn nicht selbst dieselbe in sich hat.
e: Medicines must in general be regarded as something indigestible. But the determination of indigestibility is only relative, though not in the indeterminate sense in which it is accustomed to be taken, according to which easily digestible means what weaker constitutions can tolerate. Such easily digestible matter is, for the more vigorous individuality, rather indigestible. The true relativity, that of the Concept, which has its actuality in life, consists, expressed in the quantitative regard that holds here, — in a homogeneity all the higher the higher and more independent the opposition is; the highest qualitative [p. 202] form of it in the living being has shown itself to be the relationship of the sexes, in which independent individualities are as identical. — For the lower animal formations, which have come to no difference within themselves, the neutral that is without individuality, water, is the digestible, as it is for the plant; — for children the digestible is partly the wholly homogeneous animal lymph, mother’s milk, something already digested, or rather only immediately and in general transformed into animality and not further differentiated within it itself; — partly, of different substances, those that have matured least toward individuality. Substances of this kind are, on the other hand, indigestible for natures that have grown strong. For these, by contrast, animal substances, as the individualized, or the vegetable juices ripened by light to a more vigorous self and called spiritual for that reason, are something more digestible than, e.g., the vegetable products, which are still in the merely neutral color and stand closer to the peculiar chemism. Through their more intensive selfhood those substances make an opposition all the stronger; but precisely thereby they are more homogeneous stimuli. — The medicines are, all of them, negative stimuli, poisons, something exciting and at the same time indigestible, insofar as the organism that has become estranged from itself in disease has the drive to direct itself against something foreign external to it, and thereby to attain once more the self-feeling of its individuality. — However empty a formalism Brownianism has been, if it is supposed to be the whole system of medicine, and restricts the determination of diseases and of the efficacy of remedies, the former to sthenia and asthenia and perhaps also to direct and indirect asthenia, the latter to strengthenings and weakenings, — both [p. 203] even to carbon and nitrogen and also with oxygen and hydrogen, or to a magnetic, electrical and chemical moment, and suchlike formulas that are supposed to make it natural-philosophical, it has nevertheless surely had the two important consequences: first, that through it the view of the merely particular and specific, of diseases as well as of remedies, has been broadened, and in it the universal has rather been cognized as the essential; second, that it has shown, both through its opposition to the previous, on the whole more asthenic and asthenizing manner, and through its own later transitions, that the organism does not react to the most opposed kind of treatment in so opposed a way, but frequently in a way that is at least the same in the final results, and therefore in a general way, and proves its simple identity with itself as its true essence against a particular entanglement of individual ones of its systems in specific stimuli. §. 296. The overcoming, however, and the passing off of individual inadequacies of the animal individual to its Concept does not sublate the universal inadequacy which it has thereby, that its Idea is the immediate one, or that the animal stands within nature, its subjectivity in itself the Concept but not for itself, and exists only as immediate singularity. That inner universality is therefore, against this actuality, a negative power, by which it suffers violence and perishes, because its determinate being does not itself have the same within itself.

Aber die Subjectivität des Lebendigen eben ist so wesentlichan sich mit dem concreten Allgemeinen der, Gattung identisch Ihre Identität mit dieser . daher ist nur das Aufheben des formellen Gegensaßes, der Unmittelbarkeit und der Allgemeinheit der Individualität. Indem diese Subjectivität ferner in der Idee des Lebens der Begriff ist, so ist sie an sich das absolute In sich seyn der Wirklichkeit, und durch das aufgezeigte Aufheben ihrer Unmittelbarkeit, ist sie mit sich selbst absolut zusammengegangen und das lekte Aussersich seyn der Natur aufgehoben. Die Natur ist hiemit in ihre Wahrheit übergegangen, in die Subjectivität des Begriffs, deren Objectivität selbstdie auf- - gehobene Unmittelbarkeit der Einzelnheit die concrete, Allgemeinheit der Begriff welcher den Begriff ist, sei zu nem Daseyn hat, in den Geist.
e: §. 297. This negative universal, as the abstract, is an external actuality, which exercises mechanical violence against the animal and destroys it. As its own concrete universality it is the genus, in whose process the living being, on the one hand, in copulation, sinks its different singularity; but on the other hand immediately sublates its inadequacy with the same, which is its original disease and the innate germ of death, in that it forms its singularity into the same, but because this is immediate, thereby attains only an abstract objectivity, dulls the activity, ossifies, and so kills itself out of itself. §. 298. But the subjectivity of the living being is just as essentially in itself identical with the concrete universal, the genus. Its identity with this is therefore only the sublating of the formal opposition, of the immediacy and of the universality of individuality. Since this subjectivity, further, is in the Idea of life the Concept, it is in itself the absolute being-within-itself of actuality, and through the demonstrated sublating of its immediacy it has absolutely gone together with itself and the last being-outside-itself of nature is sublated. Nature has thereby passed over into its truth, into the subjectivity of the Concept, whose objectivity itself is the sublated immediacy of singularity, the concrete universality, the Concept which has the Concept as its determinate being, — into spirit.

In dieser Wahr heit, seinem Begriffe ist die Natur verschwunden, und er hat sich als die Idee ergeben, deren Object ebenso wohl als das Subject der Begriff Diese Iden ist. = tität absolute Negativität weil ist der Natur, in der Begriff seine vollkommene äusserliche Objectivität hat diese seine Entäusserung aber aufgehoben und, er in, dieser sich identisch mit sich geworden ist. Er ist diese Identität somit nur, als Zurückkommen aus der Natur. §. 300. Das Wesen des Geistes deswegen die Frey istheit die Identität der absoluten Negativität des Be-, griffesmit sich Er kann von allem Aeusserlichen und. von seiner eigenen Seusserlichkeit, seinem Seyn abstrac hiren, und die Negation seiner individuellen Unmittelbarkeit, den unendlichen Schmerz ertragen, d.i. in dieser Negativität identisch für sich seyn. Diese Möglichkeit ist Ansich seyn sein selbstisches, sein einfa- cher Begriff oder die absolute Allgemeinheit selbst.
e: C. §. 299. Spirit has for us nature as its presupposition, of which it is the truth. In this truth, its Concept, nature has disappeared, and spirit has resulted as the Idea whose Object as well as whose subject is the Concept. This identity is absolute negativity, because in nature the Concept has its complete external objectivity, but this its externalization is sublated, and in it the Concept has become identical with itself. Spirit is this identity, therefore, only as a return out of nature. §. 300. The essence of spirit is therefore freedom, the identity of the absolute negativity of the Concept with itself. It can abstract from everything external and from its own externality, its being, and can endure the negation of its individual immediacy, infinite pain, i.e., be identical for itself in this negativity. This possibility is its self-like being-in-itself, its simple Concept, or absolute universality itself. §. 301.

o: §. 301. Diese Allgemeinheit ist aber auch sein Daseyn. Der Begriff ist das Augemeine, als sich besonderno [p. 206] des Geistes ist daher die Manifestation. Er ist nicht eine Bestimmtheit in sich gegen seine Neusserlichkeit, so daß er nicht Etwas offenbart, sondern seine Bestimmte. heit und Inhalt ist dieses Offenbaren selbst. Seine Möglichkeit ist daher unmittelbar unendliche, absolute Wirklichkeit. §. 302. Das Offenbaren ist das Seßen seiner Objectivität, welches in der abstracten Idee als unmittelbarer Uebergang Werden der Natur ist . Aber das Offenba- ren als des Geistes, der frey ist, ist Seken der Natur als seiner Welt; ein Sehen, das als Reflexion zugleich Voraussehen der Welt als selbstständiger Natur.ist Aber das wahrhafte Offenbaren das Offenbaren im Begriffe Erschaffen derselben als seines Seyns, ist, in welchem er die Positivität und Wahrheit seiner Freyheit hat -. Das Absolute ist der Geist; dieß ist dieß die hbchste Definition des Absoluten. Diese De- finition zu finden und ihren Inhalt zu begreifen, dieß kann man sagen war die absolute Tendenz al-, - ler Bildung und Philosophie auf diesen Punkt hat, sich alle Religion und Wissenschaft gedrängt aus; ihm allein ist die Weltgeschichte zu begreifen. Aber das Wesen des Geistes ist der Begriff. Das Wort und die Vorstellung des Geistes früh ist gefunden, und der Inhalt der christlichen Religion Dist, Gott als Geist offenbaren zu Diess was hier. der Vorstellung gegeben und was an sich das, Wesen in eigenen Bezu ist seinem Elemente, dem griffe,, fassen, ist die Aufgabe der Philosophie, welche so lange nicht wahrhaft und immanent gelöst ist, als der Begriff und die Freyheit nicht ihr Gegenstand und ihre Seele ist.
e: But this universality is also its determinate being. The Concept is the universal as particularizing itself [p. 206] and identity with itself in this determinacy; the nature of spirit is therefore manifestation. It is not a determinacy within itself against its externality, so that it does not reveal Something, but its determinacy and content is this revealing itself. Its possibility is therefore immediately infinite, absolute actuality. §. 302. The revealing is the positing of its objectivity, which in the abstract Idea, as immediate transition, is becoming of nature. But the revealing as that of spirit, which is free, is the positing of nature as its world; a positing that, as reflection, is at the same time the presupposing of the world as independent nature. But the true revealing, the revealing in the Concept, is the creating of it as its being, in which it has the positivity and truth of its freedom. The absolute is spirit; this is the highest definition of the absolute. — To find this definition and to comprehend its content, this one may say, was the absolute tendency of all culture and philosophy, to this point all religion and science have pressed; from it alone is world history to be comprehended. — But the essence of spirit is the Concept. The word and the representation of spirit was found early, and the content of the Christian religion is to reveal God as spirit. To grasp this, what is here given to representation, and what is in itself the essence, in its own element, the Concept, is the task of philosophy, which is not truly and immanently solved as long as the Concept and freedom are not its object and its soul.

e: §. 303. This Idea is the Concept of spirit; or it is this in itself, as a universal. But it is absolutely only spirit insofar as it is, for itself or as singularity, the Concept; and for itself it is essentially only insofar as it particularizes itself, has its Concept as presupposition, and relates itself to this as to its immediacy. This is nature, as the being of spirit, which is therefore its beginning. §. 304. This beginning is the first moment of its concrete Concept, which in its totality comprehends within itself a) subjective spirit; b) as objective spirit it realizes this Concept, and c) as absolute spirit it is for itself the unity of its Concept and its Objectivity. §. 305. The first two parts of the doctrine of spirit comprehend finite spirit. Spirit is the infinite Idea, and finitude has the significance of the inadequacy of the Concept and of reality, with the determination that it is a shining within it, — a semblance that it posits for itself as a limitation, in order, through the sublation of it, to have and to know freedom for itself as its essence. The various stages of the activity of spirit are stages of its liberation, in whose absolute truth the finding of its world as one presupposed, the generating of it as one posited by it, and the liberation from it are one and the same.

e: The determination of finitude is fixed chiefly by the understanding in relation to spirit and reason; it counts here not only as a matter of the understanding, but also [p. 208] as a moral and religious concern, to acknowledge this standpoint of modesty and to hold it fast as a final one, just as, on the other hand, it counts as a presumption of thinking, indeed as a madness of it, to want to go beyond it. — But it is, surely, rather the worst of the virtues, such a modesty of thinking as makes the finite into an absolute, and the most superficial of cognitions, to remain standing in the untrue. The determination of finitude has been illuminated and discussed not only here and there (cf. §§ 15, 34, 45 ff. etc.), but logic is, for the simple forms of thought of finitude, as the rest of philosophy is for the concrete forms of the same, only this showing that the finite is not, but is absolutely only a passing-over. Least of all, therefore, can it be said of reason and of spirit that they are finite. There are finite spirits — is the expression of the representation that remains standing at the untruth of immediate appearance, of what is meant, — at a being that the abstract understanding fixes through the form of abstract universality or identity. But finite spirit is as little as anything else finite, and as being itself, and infinitely less so, since another finite thing has its passing-away through an other, whereas it is spirit, the Concept and the eternal, itself that accomplishes this nullifying of the nugatory, this thwarting of vanity. — The modesty mentioned is, on the contrary, not only this vanity itself, but the higher vanity, the holding fast to vanity against the true. It will show itself in spirit itself in its development, as its highest deepening into itself and innermost turning point, as evil.

e: The question concerning the immateriality of the soul can still have an interest only if matter is represented as something true on the one hand, and spirit as a thing on the other. Even the physicists, however, have in recent times come upon imponderable stuffs such as heat, light, etc., to which they could easily reckon space and time as well. These imponderables, however, still have otherwise a sensuous determinate being, a being-outside-itself; but for the life-matter, which one can also find counted among them, there is lacking not only gravity but also every other determinate being by virtue of which it could still be reckoned among the material. In fact, in the Idea of life the being-outside-itself of nature is already sublated in itself and the Concept is its substance; but in spirit, the Concept, whose existence is not singularity as the immediate, but as absolute negativity, freedom, this being-outside-itself is entirely volatilized into the subjective reality of the Concept, into [p. 211] universality. — Another question connected with this is that concerning the community of the soul and the body. It was assumed as a fact, and the only point at issue was therefore how it is to be comprehended? What can be regarded as the usual answer is that it is an incomprehensible mystery. For in fact, if both are presupposed as absolutely independent of one another, they are just as impenetrable to one another as any matter is assumed to be impenetrable to another and to be found only in their reciprocal non-being, their pores. But the answer that all philosophers have given, since this relationship became a question, cannot be regarded as equivalent to this answer. Descartes, Malebranche, Spinoza, Leibniz have all alike given God as this relation, and indeed in the sense that the finite soul and matter have no truth, so that God is not merely another word for that incomprehensibility, but rather the true identity of them. — This identity, however, is not yet to be grasped here immediately as God, for it does not yet have this determination, but as yet only that of natural spirit, or of the soul itself as universal soul, in which matter is in its truth, as a simple thought or as a universal. — This soul, however, must not itself be fixed again, say, as world-soul, for it is only the universal substance, which has actual truth only as singularity. §. 310.

This subjectivity, however, comes into consideration here only as individuation of the natural determinacy; it is, as the mode of the different temperament, character, physiognomy and other dispositions of families or of the singular individuals. §. 315. β) The immediate judgment is the awakening of the individual soul, which, at first as natural determinacy and state, confronts its unconscious natural life, a state, sleep. This transition of individuality is connected with the universal body of individuality, the earth. §. 316. Awakening is not distinguished from sleep for us or externally; rather, awakening is itself the judgment of the individual soul, and thus the distinguishing of itself from its undifferentiated universality. Into wakefulness falls, in general, all self-conscious and rational activity of spirit. — Sleep is a strengthening of this activity, not as a rest from it (living activity, considered as force, rather slackens in the lack of its expression), but as a return from the world of determinacies, of dispersion, and from the becoming fixed in the singularities, into the universal essence of subjectivity, which is the absolute power.

e: The progression of the universal soul to the still immediate singularity is in general the progression of the natural Idea, from ideal universality to vitality, which is organic individuality. This has no further significance than that it has spirit indwelling within it in itself, and is the singular and natural determinate being of spirit, which, however, is therefore here as yet only in outer representation. Whatever more specific things can therefore be said, as before, of wakefulness as a specific wakefulness of spirit, and of the course of the ages of life in the peculiar significance of spiritual development, must be regarded as anticipated or as taken from representation. — Into the natural side of this immanence of the singular spirit in its corporeity there falls, in general, its healthy sympathetic co-living with it. Included under this are not only the outer feelings of the senses considered above (§ 279), but more specifically the more determinate, immediately symbolizing sensations, that colors, smells, tones are immediately agreeable or repugnant, in a more universal or in an idiosyncratic manner. To inner sympathy it belongs that desire in general is felt in the system of reproduction, [p. 215] anger and courage in the breast, the seat of the irritable, and reflective thinking, spiritual occupation, in the head, the seat of the sensible system. b. §. 319. The soul, which at first lives immediately in its substantial identity, is in its individuality the negative relation to itself, and the division of its subjectivity against its substantial life, which is inadequate to its Concept. This first reflection-into-itself is at the same time reflection-into-another; it therefore stands at first only in relationship to its natural determinacy. §. 320. The subject is α) in abstract universal relationship to its natural life; the soul is indeed subject in this judgment, but its predicate in this universal relation is still its substance, and it is an impotent, merely formal being-for-itself, the intimating and dreaming of its more universal natural life, the feeling of the natural spirit.

e: This relationship stands at the parting of the ways of spirit from itself as soul. Spirit as such has the universal for its object as something thought, i.e., as something purely identical with its abstract subjectivity, I-hood, and its relation to it is itself this thinking. This higher substantiality is freedom, the pure negativity of all immediacy. But the substantiality of the universal soul is the immediate, merely positive identity, not the free one, which [p. 216] self-consciousness and purely actual spirit already have. The present, not free stage is therefore a lowering of free self-consciousness, — a disease, in which the soul, according to Plato as prophesying, into the liver, more precisely into the ganglia as the brain of the abdomen, spirit in general into natural spirit, has sunk back. — In history this magical relationship, which can occur in single individuals as a state of disease, constitutes a stage of the transition from substantial spirituality to what is self-conscious and of the understanding. — Intimations, prophecies, much of the wondrous in dreaming and other things, somnambulism and animal magnetism, belong more or less in this sphere of dreaming in general, on which spirit wavers between its natural spirit and its rational actuality, and brings its more universal connection, in a greater breadth of nature, to representation than does the consciousness that has come to understand itself and is rational. — But since only to this consciousness the proper universality, namely that of thinking, belongs, that extension of sympathetic life which comes to representation is absolutely restricted to a particular circle, and what this soul sees and has intimations of is only its particular inwardness, not that of the universal essence; likewise, because the soul has been lowered from its free universality to particularity, this magic circle is a being-bound, a dependence, an enchantment. — The representation of a primitive state of man, in which, before his inner intuition, nature and spirit had stood not in external immediacy but in their laws and Ideas, [p. 217] is therefore, as with the few circumstances of tradition which have been interpreted in that sense and which dwindle together daily to ever greater meagerness, an empty assumption, in which the universal nature of the Idea, of being rational thought, which belongs only to spirit in its free subjectivity, is not heeded. §. 321. β) The subjective soul, however, as such breaks this immediate, substantial identity of the relationship with its particular natural being. Its opposition, but at the same time as an identity, is a relationship of contradiction; — a state of disruption, in which, since in this relationship the two that are distinguished are, as actual ones, against one another, corporeal actuality becomes the actuality of the soul, or conversely the soul makes its own actuality into the corporeal one.

e: This relationship is the state of madness in general. In this connection it is 1) to be noted that this, as well as the magical relationship, are merely ideal moments, untrue relationships, and therefore have determinate being only as states and as diseases of spirit. — Just as everything finite in general, and more specifically, e.g., the formal judgment and the formal syllogism, are without truth and only the abstract moments of the objective Concept that are in themselves; hence they have only a violent determinate being, which is grounded in a destruction, — a destruction which here the understanding effects, because it transforms the concrete into abstractions and is alone their actuality, — so the relationships that have now emerged are only the ideal moments of spirit free in being, which alone is their truth. They are the individual soul, insofar as it is in the relationship of the categorical and of the [p. 218] hypothetical judgment, — still related substantially to its substance in its self-differentiating subjectivity, and just as essentially the contradiction in this relation, its being rather not its being, but the being of its other. 2) Spirit is determined at this stage of the relationship as a thing, and more precisely actually as that which is understood by soul. Among the ancients, where the opposition of thinking and being had not yet attained this determination of actuality, the soul had the more indeterminate significance of spirituality. In more recent representation and metaphysics, on the other hand, spirit as soul in general has become a thing of many properties and forces, which has been fixed more precisely in the ghost, in angels, and even furnished with color as a sensuous thing. Metaphysics has held fast to the abstract determination thing, and has therefore subjected the soul in and for itself to the determinations of being, of quality and quantity, and to the determinations of reflection of single substance, cause, etc.; here the question of the seat of the soul, of the community of this thing with the other thing, the body, has been of interest. — It is to be counted as a merit of Kant to have freed metaphysics from spirit as a thing, thus from the soul, and, what is the same, spirit from this metaphysics and from representation, and to have put the I in its place. Of spirit as a thing one can speak only in the relationship, i.e., at the stage of reflection, where it indeed dirempts its immediate substantiality or its existent universality, and determines itself for differentiation from it and as subject, but is still entangled with this being and therefore has not yet attained its [p. 219] true actuality. 3) The differences of madness — insanity, folly, raving, imbecility — are shadings which, given the determinacy that they have against one another, retain much that is indeterminate, as even against states that are allowed to pass for states of a healthy understanding. As important as their distinction is for the treatment of these diseases, it is itself just as perverse to want to draw from them, as also from the crimes and the other dregs and depravity of human beings, above all the knowledge of man. To cognize those aberrations presupposes, rather, the Concept, i.e., what man ought to be, already. — Moreover, in all those forms the disease is to be regarded not so much as a loss of understanding, but rather properly as what madness declares, as the absolute misfortune of the contradiction, that spirit, which is the free identity of the subjective and the objective, does not exist in its I-hood as absolute ideality, but as an actual thing, and just so the objective exists over against it, and it is at the same time the pure identity of these. It is thus the relationship of necessity or of finite reciprocal action, of immediate confusion and inversion; to grasp fate purely as blind fate, i.e., as absolute foreignness to the Concept, and yet to know it as such, as identical with itself, in one as its own and as not its own, is this madness. — Distraction can be regarded as the beginning of madness; in it spirit is within itself, and has no presence in its corporeity, and since this is nevertheless in it, it inverts this into its particular actuality and conversely. The highest stage is malice, in that the singularity of I-hood, [p. 220] arbitrary will in its pure abstraction, fixes itself against the objective Idea into an unfluid actuality and confuses itself with the pure will. — Psychical treatment rests on the insight that madness is not loss of reason, either on the side of intelligence or of the will, but only madness, that the treatment therefore presupposes the sick person as something rational and has in this the firm hold by which it can grasp him. §. 322. γ) The soul, however, as the Concept universal for itself, is the substantiality, the overarching power and the fate of the other actuality, which is essentially its own immediacy. Its relationship in the judgment is therefore to sublate the form of this and to posit it as its own. §. 323. Because it is original identity with this corporeity, and has its reality in it, its activity on it is not directed hostilely as against an external Object. An injury to organic life and a hostile, devastating treatment of corporeity would rather make the latter into an objectivity negative toward the subject, and thereby into a power and a fate, and would displace the standpoint of spirit. §. 324. The activity of the soul against the body is rather to posit its identity in itself with its corporeity, to sublate only the form of immediacy of this unity, and, as universal pervading soul, to be for itself in its body, subject in it as in the predicate.

e: §. 325. It therefore forms itself into the body, which it has by nature (§ 318). In this immediate being it brings forth its universality through repetition of the actions determined by its end, through induction. Thus it recollects itself in it, on the one hand, in such a way that this its identity with it is determined by it and is its subjective unity with itself. On the other hand, it has being in it, a being that, as its own, as universal, is habit, and determinate habit, skill. It masters the body as this instrument thoroughly formed by it. c. §. 326. In its thoroughly formed corporeity the soul is as singular subject, and this corporeity is the externality as predicate of it, which therein relates only itself to itself. This externality thus does not represent itself, but the soul, and is its sign. The soul is actual as this identity of the inner and the outer, and has its free shape, and human, pathognomic and physiognomic expression, only in its corporeity.

e: To the first belongs, e.g., the upright shape in general, the formation, in particular, of the hand, as the absolute tool, of the mouth, laughing, weeping, etc., and the spiritual tone poured out over the whole, which makes the body immediately known as the externality of a higher nature. This tone is such a slight, indeterminate and unsayable modification because spirit, identical with its externality, is universal and therefore just as free in it, but this at the same time has the imperfection [p. 222] of being an immediate and natural one, and is therefore a sign, which represents spirit thereby indeed, but at the same time as an other, not as it is for itself, as universal. For the animal, therefore, the human shape is the highest, as spirit appears to it. Or for spirit it is the first appearance of the same, because it is its first actuality, still immersed in the sphere of immediacy. — Spirit is therefore, in this its sign, absolutely finite and singular; it is indeed its existence, but at the same time, in its physiognomic and pathognomic determinacy, it is something contingent for it, and to want to raise physiognomy, and still more cranioscopy, to sciences is one of the emptiest notions there could be, still emptier than a signatura rerum [signature of things], if from the shape of plants their healing powers were to be cognized. §. 327. In and for itself matter has no truth in spirit, as the universal soul; corporeity, which is at first nothing but the form of immediacy, can therefore offer no resistance at all to its forming itself into it. Through this first forming-into-itself of being, spirit, since it has opposed it to itself, sublated it and determined it as its own, has lost the significance of soul, and is I. §. 328.

e: This infinity of spirit as relation of itself to itself in its immediacy, whose sublation, which has resulted, the first, which is thus still a moment, but is determined against and in this infinity as an other, is a higher awakening of it; closed together with itself in otherness, [p. 223] it is determined as singularity, which is subject for itself, and resolves itself as this negativity. The I is the infinite relation of spirit to itself, but as subjective, as certainty of itself. As this absolute negativity it is the identity in its otherness; the I is it itself and reaches over the Object, is one side of the relationship and the whole relationship; — the light that manifests itself and something else besides. §. 330. Spirit, which as soul is in the form of substantial universality, of the gravity that is within itself, is related, as subjective reflection into itself, to something dark, and consciousness is, like the relationship in general, the contradiction of the independence of the sides, and of their identity, in which they are sublated. §. 331. The Object, as released in its judgment out of the infinite reflection of spirit into itself, has this infinite relation to itself as its essence, and is determined as something existent and given against the being-for-itself of the I.

e: §. 332. Since the I is not as the Concept, but as formal identity, the dialectical movement of consciousness is for it not as its activity, but is in itself, i.e., for it an alteration of the Object. Consciousness therefore appears different according to the diversity of the given object, and its further formation as a further formation of the Object; the consideration of the necessary alteration of this, however, the Concept, falls within us, since it is still inner as such. The Kantian philosophy can be regarded most determinately in this way: that it has grasped spirit as consciousness, and contains, entirely, only determinations of the phenomenology, not of the philosophy of it. It regards the I as relation to a thing-in-itself lying beyond, so both intelligence and the will, and when, in the concept of the reflecting power of judgment, it does come to speak of the Idea of spirit, subject-objectivity, an intuitive understanding, etc., as also of the Idea of nature, this Idea itself is again reduced to an appearance, namely to a subjective maxim. It is therefore to be regarded as a correct sense of this philosophy that it was grasped by Reinhold as a theory of consciousness, under the name faculty of representation. The Fichtean philosophy has the same standpoint, and the not-I is only as object of the I, only determined in consciousness; it remains as infinite check, i.e., as thing-in-itself. Both philosophies therefore show that they have come not to the Concept or to spirit as it is in and for itself, but only as it is in relation to an other.

e: §. 333. The goal of spirit as consciousness is to make this its appearance identical with its essence, to raise the certainty of itself to truth. The existence that it has in consciousness is the formal or universal one as such; because the Object is determined only abstractly as its own, or because it is reflected in the object only into itself as abstract I, this existence still has a content that is not as its own. §. 334. The stages of this raising of certainty to truth are that it is a) consciousness in general, which has an object as such, b) self-consciousness, for which the I is the object, c) unity of consciousness and self-consciousness, in that spirit intuits the content of the object as itself and itself as determined in and for itself; — reason, the Concept of spirit. a. §. 335. Consciousness is 1) at first the immediate one, its relation to the object therefore the simple unmediated certainty of it; the object itself is, as existent, but as reflected into itself, further determined as immediately singular; — sensuous consciousness.

e: To sensuousness belong, indeed, as content the determinations of feeling, outer or inner, and as form, the spatial and the temporal. But both of these belong to spirit in its concrete form, its feeling and intuition. Consciousness as relationship contains only the [p. 226] determination of the Object that enters into relationship with the abstract I as such, the first or immediate one, therefore only as existent, and immediacy as determined in and for itself, something, existing thing, singular. What the Object otherwise is in its concretion concerns spirit; the I as concrete is spirit. Also the determinations of feeling are sensuous only through the form of immediacy; their content can be of quite another nature. The I is in consciousness still abstract thinking, and therefore has in its object at first those abstract determinations of thought. Spatial and temporal singularity is Here and Now, as in my Phenomenology of Spirit (Bamberg 1807), p. 25 ff., I have determined the object of sensuous consciousness. It is taken more essentially only according to the identity of the relationship, through which it has its determination; through this same identity it is only for consciousness as an external, not for itself external or itself a being-outside-itself. This freedom the other can obtain only through the freedom of spirit. §. 336. The sensuous as something becomes an other; the reflection of something into itself, the thing has many properties, and the singular in its immediacy manifold predicates. The many singulars of sensuousness thus become something broad, — a manifold of relations, determinations of reflection, and universalities. Since the object is thus altered, sensuous consciousness has become perceiving.

The closer stage of consciousness, at which the Kantian philosophy grasps spirit, is perceiving, which is in general the standpoint of our ordinary consciousness and, more or less, of the sciences. One starts from sensuous certainties of individual apperceptions or observations, which are supposed to be raised to truth in that they are considered in their relationship, reflected upon, in general in that they, according to determinations of the understanding, become at the same time something universal, experiences. §. 338. This connection of the singular and the universal is a mixture, because the singular is the being that lies at the ground, but the universal, by contrast, is reflected into itself. It is therefore the many-sided contradiction; — in general, of the singular things of sensuous apperception, which are supposed to make up the ground of universal experience, and of universality, which is rather supposed to be the essence and the ground, — and that of the singularity of the things themselves, which constitutes their independence, and of the manifold properties, which are rather, free from this negative bond and from one another, independent universal matters.

e: §. 353. It is a struggle; for I cannot know myself as myself in the other, insofar as the other is an immediate other determinate being for me. I am therefore directed toward the sublation of this immediacy. But it is at the same time the determinate being of self-consciousness, in which it has, as in its sign and tool, its own self-feeling and its being for others, and its universality that mediates it with them. Equally, I cannot be recognized as immediate, but only insofar as I sublate immediacy in myself and thereby give determinate being to my freedom. §. 354. The struggle of recognition therefore goes for life and death; each of the two self-consciousnesses puts the life of the other in danger and itself goes into it, — but only as in danger, for each is just as much directed toward the preservation of its life, as an essential moment. The death of the one, which resolves the contradiction on one side, through the abstract, hence crude negation of immediacy, is on the essential side, the determinate being of recognition, thus the greater contradiction. §. 355. Since life is as essential as freedom, the struggle ends — since in this sphere the immediate singularity of the two self-consciousnesses is presupposed — at first with the inequality that the one of the combatants prefers life and preserves itself as abstract or singular self-consciousness, but gives up its being-recognized, while the other, however, holds fast to this universality, and is recognized by the first as by one subjected: — the relationship of mastery and servitude.

e: Reason is therefore determined in and for itself as pure singularity of subjectivity, and therefore the [p. 235] certainty that the determinations of self-consciousness are just as much objective, determinations of the essence of things, as its own thoughts. §. 362. The peculiar determinacy that it has here, after the Object presupposed over against the I, as well as the I that is self-like over against the Object, has sublated its one-sidedness, — is the substantial truth, whose determinacy is the pure Concept that is for itself, the I, — the certainty of itself as infinite universality. Spirit has shown itself to be the unity of the soul and of consciousness, — of that simple immediate totality, and of this knowing, which, limited by no object, no longer stands in relationship, but is knowing of the simple totality, neither subjective nor objective. Spirit therefore begins only from its own being, and relates itself only to its own determinations. §. 364.

e: The soul is finite insofar as it is determined immediately or by nature; consciousness insofar as it has an object; spirit, insofar as it has immediately a determinacy within itself, or insofar as it is one posited by it. In and for itself it is the absolutely infinite, objective reason, which is its [p. 236] Concept and whose reality is knowing, or intelligence. The finitude of spirit therefore consists, more precisely, in this, that knowing has not grasped the being-in-and-for-itself of reason. But this is infinite only insofar as it is absolute freedom, and therefore presupposes itself to its knowing as immediate being-determined and thereby makes itself finite, and is the eternal motion to sublate this immediacy and to comprehend itself. §. 365. The progression of spirit is development, because its existence, knowing, the being-determined in and for itself, the end or the rational, and the translating is purely only this formal transition into manifestation. Insofar as knowing is infinite negativity, this translating in the Concept is creation in general. Insofar as knowing is as yet only abstract or formal, spirit in it is not in accordance with its Concept, and its goal is to bring forth the absolute fulfillment and the absolute freedom of its knowing. §. 366. The way of spirit is a) to be theoretical, to have to do with its immediate determinacy and to posit it as its own; — or to free knowing from the presupposition and thereby from its abstraction, and to make the determinacy subjective. Since knowing is determined within itself in and for itself, or is as free intelligence, it is immediately b) will, practical spirit, which at first wills immediately, and frees its determination of will from its subjectivity, so that it is as free will, and objective spirit.

e: The doctrine of spirit is usually treated as empirical psychology, and spirit regarded as a collection of forces and faculties, which are contingently found alongside one another, so that one and the other, without detriment to the rest, could just as well not be there; just as one does not see in physics that much indeed would be lacking to nature if, e.g., such an appendage as magnetism is represented to be were not found in it. — The relation of the faculties to one another is moreover regarded as an external necessity or purposiveness, and this usefulness of the faculties thereby often appears as a very remote, indeed even sometimes tasteless one. Psychology belongs, like logic, to those sciences which in more recent times have drawn the least benefit from the more general cultivation of spirit and the deeper Concept of reason, and is in a most wretched state. On the other side, a greater importance has indeed been attached to it by the turn of the Kantian philosophy, so much so that it, and indeed in its empirical state, is supposed to make up the foundation of metaphysics, which is said to consist in nothing other than the facts [p. 238] of human consciousness, and indeed as facts, as they are given, empirically to apprehend and to analyze them. With this position of psychology, which is at the same time mixed up with the standpoint of consciousness and with anthropology, nothing has changed for its state itself, but only this has been added, that also for metaphysics and for philosophy in general, as for spirit as such, renunciation has been made of the cognition of the necessity of that which is in and for itself, of the Concept and of the truth. §. 368. Intelligence finds itself determined; but as knowing it is this: to have what is found as its own, because it is in itself reason, to be it for itself, and to make its objectivity, which is in and for itself, subjective. Intelligence is therefore not receptive, but essentially active, in sublating the empty form of finding its reason, or in elevating the purely formal knowing, which it is as the finding-itself of reason, to determinate knowing of itself. The manner of this elevation is, because it is reason, itself rational, and a necessary transition, determined by the Concept, of one determination of its activity into the other.

e: will, for only free self-determination is will, as the will is intelligence, for freedom is only as the certainty of myself, in the immediate, in-itself-being determination. Thus the will will show itself as the truth of intelligence, or rather intelligence will show the will itself as its truth. The will of spirit to be as intelligence is its self-determination, to abstract from its ends, interests, posited by it, and not to behave as will. — The most trivial form of that false separation is the imagined possibility that, as it is called, the understanding could be cultivated without the heart and the heart without the understanding. Such an opinion is the abstraction of the contemplative understanding, which holds fast to such distinctions; just as it is the actual understanding in the individual that separates it in this way, brings it into the untruth of spiritual determinate being and fixes it therein, — an understanding that is just as much will. But it is not philosophy that is supposed to take such untruths of determinate being and of representation for the truth. — A multitude of other forms, which are used of intelligence, that it receives impressions from outside, takes them up, that representations arise through effects of external things as the causes, etc., belong to the standpoint of perceiving, of the mixture of sensuous determinations and determinations of the understanding (§ 336), a standpoint that does not befit spirit, still less philosophizing. — That intelligence appears determined in an infinitely manifold, contingent manner is likewise the standpoint of the wholly finite singularity and of the extreme untruth of the empirical natural life of the individual soul. 2) A particularly [p. 240] favored form of reflection is that of the forces and faculties of the soul, of intelligence or of spirit. — As regards the faculty, the dynamis has in Aristotle a quite different meaning, — it designates the in-itself-being and is distinguished from entelechy, as activity, being-for-itself, actuality. The faculty, however, like force, is represented as the fixed determinacy of the content, as reflection-into-itself. Force (§ 85) is indeed the infinity of form, of the inner and the outer; but its essential finitude constitutes the indifference of the content toward the form (ibid. Remark). Herein lies the reasonless, which is brought by this form of reflection and by the consideration of spirit as a multitude of forces into it, as also into nature. What can be distinguished in its activity is held fast as an independent determinacy, and spirit is in this way made into an ossified, mechanical collection. If a force of spirit is considered in and for itself, i.e., its content, the particular determinacy which it contains, then it proves itself as determinacy, i.e., as dialectical and passing over, not as independent; thus the very form used, of a force, which is supposed rather to be the reflection-into-itself of the determinacy and fixes it into independence, sublates itself. With this the Concept enters, in which the forces vanish. — This Concept and the dialectic is intelligence itself, the pure subjectivity of the I, in which the determinacies are as fluid moments, and which is the absolutely concrete, the night of the self, in which the infinite world of representations, which each [p. 241] intelligence is, as well as the own determinations of its activity, which have been taken as forces, are sublated. As the simple identical of this manifoldness it determines itself to this simplicity of a determinacy, to the understanding, to the form of a force, of an isolated activity, and grasps itself as intuition, force of representation, faculty of the understanding, etc. But this isolating and the abstractions from activities and these opinions about them are not the Concept and the rational truth of themselves. §. 369. Intelligence is, as soul, immediately determined; as consciousness it is in relationship to this determinacy as to an external Object; as intelligence it finds itself so determined; thus it is 1) feeling, the dull weaving of spirit within itself, in which it is material-like to itself, and has the whole material of its knowing. On account of the immediacy in which spirit is as feeling or sensing, it is therein absolutely only as singular and subjective. §. 370. The form of sensation is that it is indeed a determinate affection, but that this determinacy is simple, and in it the distinction, both of its content from other content and of the externality of the same from subjectivity, is not yet posited.

e: That spirit has in its sensation the material of its representations is a very general presupposition, but more usually in the opposite sense to the one that this proposition has here. For although judgment in general and the distinction of consciousness into a subject and an Object is later than simple sensation, it is nevertheless [p. 242] taken as the earlier one, and the determinacy of sensation derived from an independent, external or internal object. Here, in the sphere of spirit, this standpoint of consciousness, opposed to idealism, has perished. Feeling or sensation is, through its form, the material-like, in that it is this immediate, still within itself undifferentiated, dull knowing of spirit. — Aristotle, too, has recognized the determination of sensation, in that he recognized the sensing subject and the sensed Object, into which consciousness separates it, only as the sensing in accordance with possibility, but said of sensation that the entelechy of the sensing and of the sensed is one and the same. — No prejudice is indeed more false than that the proposition that there is nothing in thinking that has not been in the senses — and indeed in the ordinary sense mentioned above — is ascribed to Aristotle. His whole philosophy is rather the very opposite of it. — An equally common prejudice, like this historical one, is that there is even more in feeling than in thinking; this is laid down especially with regard to moral and religious feelings. — It has turned out that the material that spirit is to itself as feeling is the being-determined in and for itself of reason. But this form of its simplicity is the lowest and the worst, in which it cannot be as spirit, as something free, as infinite universality, which is its essence. It must rather absolutely go beyond this most untrue manner of its being, because, in this immediacy in which it is determined, because it only is, it is actual as something contingent, subjective, particular, not as something rational. — Therefore [p. 243] also, when a human being appeals, concerning something, not to the nature and the Concept of the matter, or at least to grounds, the universality of the understanding, but to his feeling, there is nothing else to do than to leave him standing, because he thereby withholds himself from the community of rationality, and shuts himself up in his isolated subjectivity, particularity. §. 371. The abstract, identical direction of spirit in sensation, as in all the other of its further determinations, is attention; the moment of the formal self-determination of intelligence. §. 372. This self-determination is, however, essentially not this abstract one; as infinite it dirempts the simplicity of its being-determined, and thereby sublates its immediacy. Thus it posits the same as a negative, the felt, distinguished from intelligence as reflected into itself, the subject, in which feeling is a sublated one. This stage of reflection is representation. §. 373.

The relationship of the concrete images is at first that of their external, immediate space and time, preserved along with them. — But since the image in the subject, in which it is preserved, has only the negative unity in which it is carried and its concretion is maintained, its immediate one, in which it is determined as one in sensing and intuiting, or rather in consciousness, is by contrast dissolved. The reproduced content, as belonging to the self-identical unity of intelligence, and emerging out of its inner into representation, is a universal representation, which is the associating relationship of the concrete representations.

e: The so-called laws of the association of ideas have had great interest, especially in the flourishing of empirical psychology contemporaneous with the decline of philosophy. In the first place, it is no ideas that are associated. In the second place, these modes of relating are no laws, for the very reason alone that there are so many laws concerning the same matter, whereby arbitrariness and contingency, the opposite of a law, rather obtain. The progression through images and representations according to associating imagination is in general the play of a thoughtless representing, in which the determination of intelligence is as yet the wholly formal universality, but the content is the one given in the images. — Incidentally, image and representation are distinguished only in that the former is the more concrete; representation, whether the content be a pictorial one or Concept and Idea, has in general the character of being, though something belonging to intelligence, yet according to its content something given for it and immediate. — Otherwise it is evident that, since intuition is immediate relation, the I as ideal, thereby a universality external to its reflection-into-itself, which is not yet a determination of the content, whereas representation and its reproduction is a determinate universality, — that intuiting, representing and imagination are therefore essentially thinking, though not yet liberated thinking, and the content is not a thought. — The abstraction that is in the representing activity, by which universal representations are produced, is usually expressed as a falling upon one another of many similar images and is supposed in this way to become comprehensible. In order that this falling upon one another not be wholly chance, the conceptless, there would have to be assumed an [p. 246] attractive force of the similar images or the like, which would at the same time be the negative power to rub off against one another what is still unlike in them. This force is in fact intelligence itself, the I as universal, which through its recollection immediately gives them universality. §. 377. The association of representations is therefore a subsumption of the singular ones under a universal one. This universality is at first form of intelligence. But this is just as much within itself determinate, concrete subjectivity, and its own content can be a thought, Concept or Idea. As subsuming the images under the peculiar content, intelligence is recollected in those as determinate within itself, and forms them into this its content. Thus it is phantasy, symbolizing, allegorizing or poetizing imagination. §. 378. Intelligence is completed, in the determinate recollection of phantasy, insofar as its content, taken from itself, has a pictorial existence. This recollection of intuition is memory. §. 379.

e: The sign is some immediate intuition, but one that represents a representation of quite another content than it has for itself; — the pyramid, into which a foreign soul is transposed and preserved. The sign is different from the symbol, an intuition whose own determinacy is, according to its essence and Concept, more or less the thought that it expresses as symbol. As designating, therefore, intelligence proves a freer arbitrary will and mastery in the use of intuition than as symbolizing. — Usually the sign and language are inserted somewhere as an appendix in psychology or also in logic, without any thought being given to the necessity and connection of it in the system of the activity of intelligence. Its true place is the one indicated: that intelligence, which as intuiting generates time and space, now gives its independent representations a definite determinate being, the filled space and time, uses the intuition, in the determinacy which it has from the material of sensation, as its own, effaces its immediate and peculiar representation, and gives it another one as meaning and soul. — This sign-creating activity is rightly called memory, and indeed productive memory; since memory, which admittedly in common life is often confused with recollection, [p. 248] also with representation and imagination, and used synonymously, has altogether to do only with signs. But even if it is meant in this its closer determination, usually only the reproductive memory is thought of; but intelligence essentially produces what it reproduces. §. 380. The intuition that is used for a sign is, as immediate, at first a given and spatial one. But since it is only as sublated, and intelligence is this its negativity, the truer form of the determinate being of the sign is time, — a vanishing in that it is, and the tone is the filled expression of the inwardness that makes itself known (§ 279). The tone, articulating itself further for the determinate representations, speech and its system, language, gives to sensations and intuitions a second, higher one than their immediate one, and to representations in general a determinate being that holds in the realm of representing. §. 381. The identity of the intuition in the sign and its meaning is at first the singular production; but as unity of intelligence it is just as essentially something universal. The activity of recollecting it and thereby making it universal, as well as of reproducing it, is the retaining-by-heart and reproductive memory. §. 382.

As comprehending, intelligence has the being-determined, which in its sensation was at first as immediate material, within itself as absolutely its own, and thereby not as being-determined, but as determining. In logic, thinking has been considered as it is at first in itself, then as it is for itself and as it is in and for itself, — as being, reflection and Concept and then as Idea. It therefore emerges again and again in these different parts of the science, because they are different only through the element and the form of opposition, but thinking is this one and the same center, into which, as into their truth, the oppositions return. §. 387. Thinking, because it is the free Concept, is also free as to content; the determinacy of reason is the proper one of subjective intelligence, and as determinate it is its content and determinate being. Thinking subjectivity is thus actual; its determinations are ends; it is free will.

e: If appeal is made to the feeling of right and morality that the human being has in himself, to his benevolent inclinations, etc., to his heart in general, i.e., the subject, insofar as all the different practical feelings are united in it, this has 1) the correct sense, that these determinations are his own immanent ones, 2) and then, insofar as feeling is opposed to the understanding, [p. 252] that against its one-sided abstraction it can be the totality. But feeling can just as well be one-sided, inessential, bad; through the form of immediacy it is essentially the contingent and subjective. The rational in the shape of rationality, which, on the other hand, is as something thought, is the same content that practical feeling has, but in its universality and necessity, in its objectivity and truth. For this reason it is, on the one hand, foolish to suppose that, in the transition from feeling, e.g., to right and duty, anything is lost in content and excellence; — this transition first brings feeling to its truth; — likewise, to hold intelligence to be superfluous, indeed harmful, for feeling, heart and will; the truth, and, what is the same, the rationality of the heart and will can take place only in the universality of intelligence, not in the singularity of feeling. — On the other hand, however, it is suspect, and very well more than this, to hold fast to feeling and heart against rationality as thought, because what is more in the former than in the latter is only particular subjectivity, the vain, and arbitrary will. — For the same reason it is inept, in the consideration of feelings, to go into anything more than their form, and to consider their content, since this, as thought, consists rather of the self-determinations of spirit in their universality and necessity, rights and duties. §. 391.

e: What holds of the inclinations is quite the same as what holds of the feelings; they are self-determinations of the will that is in itself free, but that is not yet, in the content of its self-determination as intelligence, free for itself, [p. 255] not yet universal and objective. Passion already contains this in its determination: that it is restricted to a particularity of the determination of the will and to the subjective singularity, whatever its content may otherwise be. But with regard to the inclinations the question raised is rather which of them are good and evil, likewise to what degree the good ones remain good, and, since they are particular ones against one another and many in number, how they, since they are after all found in one subject, and according to experience cannot very well all be satisfied, must at least restrict one another. It is the same with these many drives and inclinations at first as with the powers of the soul, whose collection theoretical spirit is; — a collection that is now augmented by the multitude of drives. The formal rationality of the drive and of the inclination consists only in their universal drive, in this: not to be as something subjective, but to be realized. But their true rationality cannot result in a consideration of external reflection, partly not under the presupposition that they are assumed and fixed as independent natural determinations and immediate drives, partly it is rather the immanent reflection of spirit itself to go beyond their particularity and immediacy, and to give them the form of rationality and objectivity, in which they are as necessary relationships and rights and duties. It is this objectivation itself, then, that shows their import, as well as their relationship to one another, in general their truth. As Plato, what justice is in and for itself, with true sense, also insofar as he comprehended under the right of spirit its whole nature, [p. 256] showed that he could present only in the objective shape of justice, namely the construction of the state, as of the ethical life. — What, then, the good, rational inclinations and their subordination are changes into the presentation of what relationships spirit brings forth in that it sublates its subjectivity and realizes itself; — an objectivity in which precisely its self-determinations in general lose the form of inclinations, just as the content loses subjectivity, contingency or arbitrary will. §. 394. The universal in these drives is the singular subject, the activity of their satisfaction or formal rationality, namely of the translation from subjectivity into objectivity. The dialectic of this manifold, particular content is, however, the simple subjectivity of the will itself, which at first, as reflecting will, raises the contradiction of the drives into formal universality, and makes 3) happiness its end.

e: The expression natural right, which has hitherto been customary for the philosophical doctrine of right, contains the ambiguity whether right is meant as something implanted, as it were, by immediate nature, or whether it is meant as it determines itself through the nature of the thing, i.e., the Concept. That sense, however, is the one formerly customarily meant; so that at the same time a state of nature has been invented, in which natural right is supposed to hold, while the state of society and of the state demands, by contrast, rather a restriction of freedom and a sacrifice of natural rights. In fact, however, right and all its determinations are grounded solely on free personality, a self-determination, which is rather the opposite of natural determination. A state of nature is therefore a state of violence and of wrong, of which nothing truer can be said than that one is to go out of it. Society, by contrast, is the state in which alone right has its actuality; what is to be restricted and sacrificed is precisely the arbitrary will and violence of the state of nature. — The formalism of right consists in this, that it is the abstract and precisely [p. 265] thereby immediate determination of free personality; the subsumption of the particular existence under it is therefore something contingent, and which objects are my property is a matter of arbitrary will and of chance. — The transition of right into morality is therefore made by the necessity of subjectivity, but at the same time of the sublation of its contingency, whereby it becomes something universal determinate in and for itself. B. §. 416. The particularity of the person becomes, through the judgment of free personality, an essential moment. The subjective interest and the particular welfare thereby become an end on the one hand; on the other hand, the universal will that is in and for itself has its actuality through subjectivity, insofar as it, by giving up its immediacy, has the disposition, insight and intention of the good. §. 417. The moral standpoint is thereby the judgment of reflection of freedom, or the relationship in which personal subjectivity posits itself as absolutely independent, and therefore repels the moments of the will into independent extremes, — the universal rational will and an external independent world. Subjectivity is their middle term, and is just as immediately identical with them as it, because they are independent, posits itself with them and them with one another in only relative relation.

e: §. 418. The universal syllogism is that the moral subject, as the unity, being for itself, of the opposition, which is likewise independent in the extremes, is this inner contradiction and, as identity, the activity and the drive to sublate it, i.e., to act, to realize the end in one, and to make the external world accord with the end. §. 419. The action is indeed the absolute determination, through its end, of the objectivity that is selfless in relation to the free subject. But since this is also independent, it can invert the action of the individual and bring to light something other than lay in the latter. Although every alteration as such that is posited by the activity of the subject is the deed of the latter, it does not on that account recognize it as its action, but recognizes as its own only that in the deed which lay in its knowing and will; — as its guilt; — because it counts itself only as absolutely subjective and for-itself-being will. §. 420. But this universal transition, which is acting in general, still contains manifold other relative identities, α) the universal will that is in and for itself is the law and the substance, in which the immediate singularity of the subject, as well as external reality in general, is sublated; it is therefore the absolute final end, the good in and for itself; duty for the subject, and the ultimate end of the world.

But β) the good contains in its Concept, as the universal of the will, the moment of reality, which however lies in the singularity distinct from this universality, in the subjectivity of the I reflected into itself and its self-determining activity; — the subject is to have insight into the good, and make it its intention, and is to bring it forth through its activity. §. 422. γ) The good is at first as abstract-universal; but as the essential of the will it is within itself negative and therefore a particular. There are accordingly many kinds of good and many sorts of duties, whose diversity is dialectical against one another, and brings them into collision. §. 423. They are to stand in agreement, however, since each, as duty and as good, is absolute, because it has the universal will as its essence. Just so the individual, since the action is the activity of the subject and has singularity as its principle, is to know them themselves in their diversity, as well as the many sides of the objectivity presupposed by the subject as singular, of the case, which is a concrete and within itself manifold one; just so the various duties that relate to these various sides. There is to be, further, the true dialectic, which knows their subordination among one another, and resolves upon a single one or a combination of them with exclusion of the others or of their absolute validity. §. 424.

Since this choosing certainty of itself is the reflection of the abstract will, infinite to itself in its immediate singularity, it yields the two forms, passing immediately over into one another, of conscience and of evil. Evil, however, is this same knowing of its singularity as the deciding one, insofar as it does not remain in this abstraction but has against the good the content of a subjective interest. §. 428. This highest peak of the phenomenon of the will, which has been volatilized up to this absolute vanity — a being-good not objective but purely only certain of itself, and a certainty of itself in the nullity of the universal — collapses immediately in on itself. e: The free substance, in which the absolute ought is just as much being, is, as a nation, actuality. The abstract diremption of its negativity into existence is the individuation into persons, of whose immediate independence it is the inner power and necessity. The person, however, cognizes, as thinking intelligence, the substance as its own essence, and in this disposition ceases to be an accident of it; it beholds its absolute final end in actuality just as much as an attained this world, as it [p. 271] brings it forth through its activity, but as something that just as much is, it thereby fulfills, without the choosing reflection, its duty as its own and as what is, and in this necessity has itself and its freedom. §. 432. Because the substance is the absolute unity of the singularity and of the universality of freedom, the actuality and activity of every individual, to be for himself and to care, is conditioned both by the presupposed whole, in whose connection alone it is present, as well as being a passing over into a universal product. — Equally the substance and the universal work is the independence of the individuals, which is thereby brought forth. — The disposition of the individuals is the knowing of this identity of all their interests with the whole, and that the other individuals reciprocally know themselves, and are actual, only in this identity, — trust, — the true, substantial disposition. §. 433. The universal work, which is the substance itself, particularizes itself and the labor of the same into the differences which are the estates: the universal one, the enactment of the substance as such; the particular one, whose work is the needs of particular determinate being and whose nearest end is particular subjectivity, but whose attainment presupposes the labor of all others, and likewise reaches into it. The estate of singularity is individuality, insofar as it is for itself a totality, a whole that is indeed natural but, through spirituality, equally raised into ethical life, the family.
